findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: The council is using one-off resources to balance each year, with a 2025/26 outturn deficit of £7.839m and a 2026/27 Q1 forecast deficit of £8.489m
findings.detail: The 2025/26 outturn position was an outturn deficit of £7.839m, balanced using one-off resources "recognised as a part of the council's general financing. As one-off resources, they are not available to support the council's budget going forward." The 2026/27 Quarter 1 forecast reports a revenue budget deficit of £8.489m, comprising £5.715m on cash limit service budgets and £2.774m on non-cash limit corporate budgets. The General Fund Balance remains at the minimum recommended level of £15.183m. The council states: "Reserves can only provide temporary flexibility and mitigation of risk. Any sustained or substantial use of reserves and one-off funding will reduce the council's future ability to respond flexibly to emerging pressures, manage temporary risks and support other priorities and ambitions."
findings.matters: The use of reserves to balance budgets signals the underlying position is not sustainable. If one-off resources are being used year-on-year, reserves are a stopgap, not a strategic buffer. The council's minimum reserve level means there is little headroom to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn deficit £7.839m (funded from reserves); 2026/27 Q1 forecast deficit £8.489m (£5.715m services, £2.774m corporate); General Fund Balance £15.183m (minimum level)
findings.quote: The 2025/26 outturn deficit was balanced using one-off resources recognised as a part of the council's general financing. As one-off resources, they are not available to support the council's budget going forward.

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: Core Spending Power increases by only 7.53% over the settlement period, compared with 15.52% nationally and 19.7% for comparable metropolitan boroughs, a structural funding gap
findings.detail: The multi-year Local Government Finance Settlement has "materially weakened the council's financial position." Stockport's Settlement Funding Assessment reduces by around £23m by 2028/29. Core Spending Power increases by 7.53% over the settlement period, less than half the England average of 15.52% and well below the 19.7% average for metropolitan boroughs with comparable service responsibilities. Late changes worsened this further: Stockport received zero allocation from the £2.240bn national Recovery Grant and is excluded from the funding protection guarantee (5%, 6%, 7% floor in years 1-3). The council estimates it would have received around £10m over the settlement period if the Recovery Grant had been distributed by relative need.
findings.matters: This is a funding gap that local efficiency cannot close. The council cannot grow its way out of this — it is a structural allocation decision. The gap persists across the medium term and means the council is permanently worse funded than peers.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power +7.53% vs England +15.52% vs MBCs +19.7%; Settlement Funding Assessment reduces ~£23m by 2028/29; Stockport received £0m from £2.240bn Recovery Grant (would have received ~£10m by need)
findings.quote: Over the settlement period, the council's Core Spending Power increases by 7.53%, less than half the England average of 15.52% and well below the 19.7% average for metropolitan borough councils, which have comparable service responsibilities and demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: SEND transport demand increased 58% in four years (1,243 pupils at June 2026 vs ~786 in June 2022), with limited tools to arrest growth
findings.detail: The number of pupils requiring special school transport increased from approximately 786 in June 2022 to 1,243 in June 2026. The council is implementing cost-control measures (independent travel training, shared routes with neighbours, policy alignment with Greater Manchester authorities, increased scrutiny of hackney carriage fares) and notes opportunities from the GM Our Pass scheme for 11-16 year-olds from January 2027. However, the paper explicitly states that "any reduction in demand or cost will depend on the timing and detail of the reforms, adequate national funding, the capacity of mainstream schools to meet a wider range of needs, and the availability of local specialist provision. The benefits are therefore likely to be realised over the longer term rather than providing immediate relief from current financial pressures."
findings.matters: SEND transport is a General Fund pressure driven by identification of need and is not easily reducible. The council's mitigations (travel training, shared routes) are marginal. The 58% growth in four years shows acceleration.
findings.figures: 1,243 pupils requiring transport at June 2026; 58% increase since June 2022
findings.quote: At June 2026, 1,243 pupils required transport, an increase of 58% since June 2022.

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: The council has nine children's placements costing over £10,000 per week (annual costs up to £887,000), driven by increasing complexity and market failure
findings.detail: Despite a 3% reduction in children in care (from 508 to 492 between June 2025 and June 2026), placement costs continue to rise. External placements increased from 29% to 31% of children in care. The council details two highest-cost cases: one young person subject to a deprivation of liberty safeguards order requiring 3:1 staffing at £17,061/week (£887,172 annually); another with complex needs requiring additional unused bed space (bed-blocking fee) at £14,538/week (£756,376 annually). Total forecast cost of these nine high-cost placements: £5.7m. The council identifies causes as "increased use of high-cost residential and independent placements, limited competition and price control in the placement market, growing complexity linked to SEND, mental health and family breakdown, and insufficient mental health provision elsewhere in the system."
findings.matters: These are individual high-cost placements that signal market failure and absence of alternatives. The trajectory of external placement growth (29% to 31%) suggests this pressure will continue. Prevention programmes exist but their effectiveness is unproven at scale.
findings.figures: 9 placements over £10,000/week; highest £17,061/week; second highest £14,538/week; total £5.7m; external placements 29% to 31%
findings.quote: The scale of these pressures is illustrated by the council's nine external placements costing more than £10,000 per week, with a total forecast cost of £5.7m. The two highest-cost placements are £17,061 per week for a young person subject to a deprivation of liberty safeguards (DoLS) order requiring 3:1 staffing, and £14,538 per week for a young person whose complex needs require additional space that cannot be used by another child, resulting in a bed-blocking fee.

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: Adult social care accounts for over 43% of the service budget, with an aging population (65+ projected to grow 11%, 85+ to grow 36% over ten years), and no funded policy solution in sight
findings.detail: Stockport is the "oldest" locality in Greater Manchester. The population aged 65+ is projected to increase by 11% over the next ten years to 69,900; the population aged 85+ is projected to rise 36% to 12,000. In March 2025, 32.3% of adults in long-term support were aged 85+, compared with 25% across comparable metropolitan boroughs. Adult social care costs continue to rise due to provider fee pressures, workforce shortages, and market capacity constraints. The council notes that "Increasing spend on adult social care is not specific to Stockport, with councils across the country experiencing increasing need and complexity of support needed, driving costs." Government reform programmes (fair cost of care, care accounts, lifetime caps) have been "repeatedly delayed," leaving councils "continuing to meet rising demand and provider cost pressures within existing budgets, while carrying the financial risk."
findings.matters: Adult social care is the single largest budget pressure and is structural — driven by demographics, not economic cycles. The council cannot reduce demand and has no funded policy solution. This pressure will persist and likely grow.
findings.figures: 43% of service budget on adult social care; 65+ population projected +11% (to 69,900); 85+ projected +36% (to 12,000); 32.3% of adults in long-term support aged 85+ vs 25% average for MBCs
findings.quote: Over 43% of the council's service budget is spent on providing essential support to older residents through adult social care services

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: The council is moving closer to the threshold for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), a form of government-administered distress funding
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states that "pressures of this scale cannot be managed indefinitely through local financial controls alone" and notes "the increasing prospect that EFS may need to be considered." The council frames this as a contingency requiring "early and prudent consideration of its timing, conditions and longer-term consequences." EFS does not resolve recurrent pressures; it defers costs into future years. The LGA has warned that 36 councils required EFS in 2026/27, signalling this is now a systemic condition rather than an exceptional one. The council's current assessment is that Section 114 remains "low" in the short term, but the trajectory is explicitly toward intervention.
findings.matters: EFS signals distress and typically carries restrictions on discretionary borrowing and service reduction mandates. For a lender, it means the council's capacity to service debt becomes a government concern, not just a council one.
findings.figures: 36 councils required EFS in 2026/27; Stockport's likelihood of Section 114 currently low but trajectory worsening
findings.quote: early and prudent consideration of its timing, conditions and longer-term consequences is necessary to preserve options and avoid a more acute financial intervention

findings.paper_title: Part A: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) Summer Review Update
findings.headline: Savings requirement escalates to £29.137m by 2030/31, up from £23.323m forecast in February
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in February set a cumulative savings requirement of £23.323m by 2029/30. This update extends to 2030/31 and revises requirements upward: £12.078m in 2027/28, £21.887m in 2028/29, £25.628m in 2029/30, £29.137m in 2030/31. These are cumulative annual targets — the council must find £12.078m in recurring savings in 2027/28, then achieve a further £9.809m in 2028/29, with the gap widening each year. The council states these "will be reviewed through the 2027/28 budget-setting process" but offers no plan for delivery.
findings.matters: Escalating unmet savings targets indicate the council cannot balance its budget through efficiency alone. Each year requires deeper cuts to services or increased dependency on one-off resources.
findings.quote: Updated MTFP assumptions and forecasts increase the savings requirement to £12.078m in 2027/28, rising to £29.137m by 2030/31

findings.headline: The peer-to-peer local authority lending market has broken; temporary borrowing is now the only option but costs have spiked
findings.detail: The council notes that liquidity shortages within local-to-local authority lending have 'intensified structurally since the 2024/25 financial year.' Short-term peer loans are now priced at 4.20%, while 364-day loans cost 4.80% plus 10bps brokerage (4.90%), which is 'practically identical to the 1-year PWLB Certainty Rate of 4.96%'. The council states this has 'completely eliminated the historical discount typically found when borrowing from peer authorities'.
findings.matters: This signals a structural shift in local authority borrowing that removes a key financing option and forces councils to choose between expensive long-term PWLB debt or expensive short-term market borrowing. It reduces financial flexibility across the sector.
findings.figures: Short-term local authority loans 4.20%; 364-day loans 4.80% plus 10bps brokerage = 4.90%; 1-year PWLB rate 4.96%
findings.quote: This supply-side contraction has completely eliminated the historical discount typically found when borrowing from peer authorities. Short-term local loans now cost 4.20%, while 364-day loans cost 4.80% plus 10bps brokerage (4.90%), practically identical to the 1-year PWLB Certainty Rate of 4.96%.

findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts have been completely overturned; long-term borrowing is now being avoided indefinitely
findings.detail: The council's treasury strategy assumed the 50-year PWLB rate would decline to 5.50% by June 2026; it instead surged to 6.35%. The Bank Rate was forecast to fall to 3.50% by June 2026; it stayed flat at 3.75%. The council now states it will reject long-term external borrowing 'at this time' and instead use temporary borrowing while internally tracking market movements. Officers acknowledge original trigger rates are 'completely unachievable' and are operating without a fixed borrowing plan.
findings.matters: This signals the council has abandoned its planned refinancing curve and shifted into reactive/tactical mode. It suggests deep uncertainty about when conditions will improve and signals the council lacks visibility on its future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: 50-year PWLB certainty rate peaked at 6.35% vs forecast 5.50%; Bank Rate held at 3.75% vs forecast 3.50%; original 5-year trigger of 4.50% vs actual 5.26%
findings.quote: The actual 50-year PWLB certainty rate climbed to an expensive peak of 6.35% during the quarter, representing a massive premium over the initial 5.50% expectation. Locking into long-term fixed debt at 6.35% remains highly punitive. This validation completely justifies the council's tactical policy to reject long-term external borrowing at this time.

findings.headline: Capital spending is running 11% ahead of budget in Q1, requiring higher borrowing
findings.detail: Capital expenditure of £169.393m in Q1 is significantly ahead of the quarterly run-rate implied by the £152.732m full-year budget. The council attributes this to re-phasing of schemes from 2025/26 being pulled forward. As a result, the in-year borrowing requirement is £63.726m vs budgeted £55.450m, an increase of £8.276m, and the Capital Financing Requirement is now £966.207m vs budgeted £959.834m.
findings.matters: Capital overspending increases the council's borrowing requirement at a time when borrowing costs are at peak rates. If this run-rate continues, the council will need to borrow substantially more than planned, adding pressure to the revenue budget.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £169.393m actual vs £152.732m budget (Q1); CFR £966.207m vs £959.834m budget; in-year borrowing requirement £63.726m vs £55.450m
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) stands at £966.207m, which is currently higher than the initial budgetary forecast, largely due to the significant re-phasing of schemes at the 2025/26 financial year end. The in-year borrowing requirement before any minimum revenue provision is £63.726m.

findings.headline: £100m of short-term debt maturing in 2026/27 cannot be refinanced at planned rates
findings.detail: The council took out £100m in short-term PWLB loans averaging 4.73% during 2024/25, betting on rates falling. Those loans now mature in 2026/27, but long-term PWLB rates surged to 6.35% (50-year). The council is rolling the debt into temporary market borrowing at 4.22%, while awaiting £61m in SEND capital funding expected October/November 2026 to ease the refinancing burden. A further £87m matures in 2027/28 at 4.87% average rate.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether Stockport can afford to refinance this debt. The council's temporary borrowing strategy defers the problem but increases refinancing risk if rates stay elevated or worsen. With £87m more maturing in 2027/28, this is a multi-year pressure.
findings.figures: £100m maturing in 2026/27 at 4.73% average; £87m maturing 2027/28 at 4.87%; temporary borrowing at 4.22%; 50-year PWLB peak rate 6.35%
findings.quote: The council paid off a maturing £20m long-term PWLB loan in June, reducing total PWLB debt from £534.992m to £514.992m. Short-Term Temporary Borrowing: to replace that cash and cover daily operations, the council took out £35m in short-term market loans from other local authorities, increasing this balance from £102.500m to £137.500m.

findings.headline: Debt service costs rising faster than expected, consuming more of the revenue budget
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream (non-HRA) increased to 10.07% compared to the 9.74% budgeted in February 2026, and the HRA ratio rose from 8.91% to 9.04%. This 0.33 percentage point increase means the council is devoting more of its annual revenue to paying interest and principal than planned, reducing funds available for services.
findings.matters: Financing cost ratios directly measure debt affordability and budget flexibility. A rising ratio signals the council is struggling under its debt burden at a time of other revenue pressures.
findings.figures: Non-HRA financing costs 10.07% actual vs 9.74% budgeted; HRA 9.04% vs 8.91% budgeted
findings.quote: The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream is 10.07% (non-HRA) and 9.04% (HRA). The forecast figures reported in the Treasury Management Strategy in February 2026 were 9.74% and 8.91% respectively.

findings.headline: SEN transport costs of £9.562m annually for 1,250 pupils across 442 routes with forecast £0.933m Q1 overspend
findings.detail: The Education service is forecasting a £0.933m deficit in Q1, driven by special educational needs transport. The council is supporting 1,250 pupils across 442 routes at an annual cost of £9.562m. Cost pressures include loss of charity providers, need for new/replacement contracts at higher price points, and complex bespoke pupil packages. The council's mitigation depends on uptake of personal budgets and a Greater Manchester free bus pass beginning January 2027 (not yet confirmed as delivering cost reduction).
findings.matters: SEN transport is a statutory, demand-led cost with limited pricing power. Rising per-pupil costs and dependency on external providers create upward pressure that cannot easily be controlled, and the mitigation (GM bus pass) is not yet proven to reduce costs.
findings.figures: £0.933m Q1 overspend, 1,250 pupils, 442 routes, £9.562m annual cost, high price inflation on new contracts
findings.quote: There is a forecast deficit at Quarter 1 of £0.933m for Education. This deficit continues to reflect the ongoing demand, challenges and cost pressures associated with the statutory requirement to provide Special Educational Needs (SEN) transport support to our most vulnerable pupils across the borough. The council is supporting 1,250 pupils over 442 routes, at an annual cost of £9.562m, highlighting the need for support, new/replacement contracts at higher price points, loss of charity not-for-profit organisations offering services and the complexity of arranging bespoke pupil packages

findings.headline: Corporate borrowing deficit of £7.573m due to high interest rates on £966m Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £7.573m deficit on corporate borrowing budgets, driven by financing costs on its capital programme and continuing high interest rates. The Capital Financing Requirement has risen to £966.207m and financing costs now consume 10.07% of the net revenue stream (up from budgeted 9.74%). The council is partially mitigating this with a £4m draw from reserves.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs in a high interest rate environment will continue to squeeze revenue budgets unless capital spending slows. The trend shows interest costs rising faster than revenues, and reserve mitigation is temporary and depletes buffers.
findings.figures: £7.573m borrowing forecast deficit, £966.207m CFR, 10.07% financing costs ratio (budgeted 9.74%), £4m reserve mitigation
findings.quote: The position includes a forecast deficit of £7.573m on the council's corporate borrowing budgets. This reflects the financing costs associated with the capital programme, together with the impact of continuing high interest rates on borrowing. As planned, the pressure is partly mitigated through the planned use of £4m from the Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation Reserve.

findings.headline: Investment & Development account portfolio losses require £4.886m emergency draw from reserves
findings.detail: The council's commercial property investment account is performing poorly due to weakness in retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The account requires £4.886m of funding from the Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation Reserve at year-end just to break even. This is separate from the £8m already drawn for DSG and represents additional erosion of the risk mitigation buffer.
findings.matters: Commercial property underperformance is reducing actual yields below budgeted income and forcing the council to choose between accepting a deficit in this account or using emergency reserves, both of which damage financial resilience.
findings.figures: £4.886m funding required from Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation Reserve, driven by national economic pressures on retail, hospitality and leisure
findings.quote: The Investment & Development (I&D) account is forecast to require £4.886m of funding from the Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation reserve at year-end to achieve a balanced position. This is mainly due to the performance of assets in the account, reflecting national economic pressures particularly on the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors.

findings.headline: Vacancy management has failed; council is covering vacant posts with expensive agency staff (10 agency social workers)
findings.detail: The frontline social work locality teams carry a £0.419m deficit and the fostering staffing team a £0.193m deficit, with the council unable to fill 10 equivalent full-time social worker posts and instead covering with agency staff. This pattern repeats across the council's staffing pressures, indicating a structural recruitment problem where the savings normally gained by vacancy management are not materialising.
findings.matters: When a council cannot fill vacancies, it loses budgeted cost savings and must pay premium rates for agency cover, effectively doubling the pressure. This signals workforce planning failure and constraints on service delivery that cannot be quickly resolved.
findings.figures: £0.419m deficit (frontline teams), £0.193m deficit (fostering), 10 agency social workers covering vacant posts
findings.quote: There are also deficits in the frontline social work locality teams, £0.419m and fostering staffing team of £0.193m, equivalent to 10 agency social workers across the two teams covering vacant posts, long-term sickness and maternity leave.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit forecast to reach £133m by March 2028, dependent on unconfirmed government grant
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £32.006m in-year DSG deficit in 2026/27. Combined with the existing £68m cumulative deficit from March 2026, this will grow to approximately £133m by March 2028 when the statutory override ends. The council expects a High Needs Stability Grant to write off 90% of the original deficit (£61m), but expects to remain responsible for approximately £13m when the override expires. This requires either reserves or capitalisation directions to resolve.
findings.matters: A £13m liability materialising in two years creates a known future funding gap. If government does not confirm the 90% write-off for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits as well, the liability could be significantly larger and rapidly exhaust remaining reserves.
findings.figures: £32.006m in-year deficit, £68m existing cumulative deficit, forecast £133m total by March 2028, estimated £61m High Needs Stability Grant, residual £13m liability
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 forecast outturn position is an in-year deficit of £32.006m...The forecast in-year deficit will be added to the council's cumulative DSG deficit of £68m at March 2026. Assuming a similar deficit in 2027/28, the cumulative balance is forecast to increase by approximately £65m to around £133m when the override ends in March 2028...this balance may need to be met from council reserves and/or capitalisation directions.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £4.177m (3.1% of budget) driven by external placement costs as high as £17,061 per week
findings.detail: The council has 9 individual children's home placements costing more than £10,000 per week, with the highest at £17,061/week for a young person requiring 3:1 staffing, and another at £14,538/week due to complex needs requiring exclusive bed access. These 9 placements alone cost £5.7m. The service is unable to control costs despite implementing a financial recovery plan that depends on opening new internal homes.
findings.matters: Runaway placement costs in statutory services indicate the council is unable to manage demand or negotiate pricing, and external dependency means costs are outside the council's direct control. A single high-cost placement change can shift the deficit materially.
findings.figures: £4.177m deficit on £136.758m budget (3.1%), 9 placements above £10,000/week, highest at £17,061/week, total high-cost placement cost £5.7m
findings.quote: We currently have 9 placements above £10,000 per week the two highest cost being, £17,061 per week for a young person on a deprivation of liberty (DoLS) order with 3:1 staffing and £14,538 for another young person which includes an additional fee due to the complex needs of the child requiring additional space, which then cannot be used by another child (a bed blocking fee). The total forecast cost of these 9 placements is £5.7m.

findings.headline: Q1 forecast deficit of £8.489m requires drawing £16.804m from reserves to balance
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a revenue deficit made up of £5.715m on cash limit service budgets and £2.774m on corporate budgets. To manage this, it is drawing £16.804m from reserves during the year, including approximately £8m from the Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation Reserve. This represents rapid depletion of financial buffers at a point where statutory service pressures are only three months into the year.
findings.matters: Persistent in-year deficits and heavy reserve reliance signal deteriorating financial resilience and reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected pressures or shocks.
findings.figures: £8.489m deficit (£5.715m cash limits, £2.774m non-cash), £16.804m reserves drawdown including ~£8m from risk mitigation reserve
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 forecast outturn position for the council's revenue budget is a deficit of £8.489m...The forecast position includes £16.804m (including around £8m of budget resilience commitments from the Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation Reserve) planned use of reserves during the year

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: The council acknowledges these pressures cannot be addressed through local financial management and efficiency alone
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's assessment, endorsed by Cabinet, states that robust financial management and local efficiency measures are insufficient to solve the gap. The council is explicit that sustainable national funding and policy reform are essential. This is a formal recognition that the council has reached the limits of internal action.
findings.matters: A lender hearing 'we cannot solve this alone' is a warning that the council may exhaust all local options and be forced to EFS or asset sales. It signals the gap is structural, not operational.
findings.figures: £29.137m gap cannot be closed by efficiency and demand management alone
findings.quote: We agree with the Section 151 Officer that these pressures cannot be addressed through robust financial management and local efficiency measures alone. Sustainable national funding and policy reform are essential

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Reserves are finite and cannot be used as a permanent solution; new reserve requests are paused
findings.detail: The council recognises that while reserves provide short-term flexibility, their sustained use cannot bridge recurrent budget pressures. New reserve requests are now paused unless they are statutory, externally ringfenced, or a clearly evidenced invest-to-save proposal with Section 151 sign-off. This policy tightening indicates the council is managing down reserve capacity.
findings.matters: Reserves are a lender's key buffer against shocks. Tightening their use signals the council views them as insufficient cover for the structural gap and is preserving them for cash-flow pressure, not using them to absorb new spending.
findings.figures: New reserve policy limits: statutory, ringfenced, or invest-to-save only
findings.quote: reserves are finite, and their sustained use cannot provide a solution to recurrent budget pressures. To safeguard this position, new reserve requests will be paused unless they relate to a statutory requirement

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Pay award of 3.3% will cost £4.1m in 2026/27 on top of other inflationary pressures
findings.detail: The 2026/27 national pay agreement was reached in August. The council's budget allocation for this cost is being reflected in Quarter 2 reporting. This is a recurrent cost that will continue into future years and compounds the savings requirement across the MTFP.
findings.matters: Pay costs are a large proportion of council spend and are outside the council's control. They add to the structural gap year on year unless offset by other savings.
findings.figures: £4.1m for 3.3% pay award in 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2026/27 national pay agreement was reached in August and confirmed a 3.3% increase. This is expected to cost the council circa £4.1m

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Adult social care, children's services, SEND transport and homelessness face severe, rising cost pressures with limited flexibility to reduce them
findings.detail: These four service areas are described as having 'limited flexibility to reduce costs' while demand and complexity grow. Adult social care faces rising need driven by an ageing population and complex younger adults; children's services sees placement costs rising despite a 3% volume reduction due to complexity; EHCP numbers and specialist transport costs are growing; homelessness is rising with acute housing shortage and increased use of temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: These are statutory, heavily inspected services the council cannot cut. Rising costs in inelastic services, combined with a funding gap, force trade-offs against discretionary services or require intervention.
findings.figures: Children in care reduced 3% but placement cost per case is rising; EHCP numbers increasing nationally and in Stockport
findings.quote: The most acute pressures are concentrated in statutory and heavily inspected services, where there is limited flexibility to reduce costs, including adult and children's social care, SEND transport, homelessness and temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: The funding settlement has materially weakened the council's medium-term financial position
findings.detail: Despite the shift to a multi-year settlement offering greater certainty, the outcome for Stockport was disappointing and did not address underlying insufficiency. The document states this has exacerbated an already challenging gap and increased the prospect of EFS. The shortfall reflects a structural mismatch between national funding and the cost of delivering statutory services.
findings.matters: This is a funding risk outside the council's control. It tells a lender that revenue-side pressures are not a temporary spike but a structural shift in the funding relationship with central government.
findings.figures: Budget gap widened following the final Local Government Finance Settlement outcome
findings.quote: the outcome for Stockport was disappointing and has materially weakened the council's medium-term financial position. The settlement has not addressed the underlying insufficiency of funding required to deliver local services

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support increasingly likely within the MTFP period
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer flags that EFS risk is increasing. While not intended for 2027/28, the council acknowledges it may become necessary in future years if service costs continue to outpace funding. The document states this risk arises from both a disappointing funding settlement and structural pressures in statutory services where demand and complexity are growing faster than available funding.
findings.matters: EFS is a formal intervention signal. A lender must treat this as material risk of government imposition of external control or rescue funding, which affects the council's autonomy and future revenues.
findings.figures: 36 councils already granted EFS for 2026/27; LGA estimates £7bn sector-wide funding gap within three years
findings.quote: We recognise that, as highlighted by the council's Section 151 Officer in the MTFP update report, the risk of EFS needing to be considered is increasing.

findings.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £29.137m by 2030/31 with no permanent solution yet identified
findings.detail: The council's MTFP review identifies a growing year-on-year gap: £12.078m in 2027/28, rising to £29.137m by 2030/31. The document describes this as 'extremely challenging' and states the gap is driven by inflationary costs, increasing service demand, and an insufficiency of national funding. Detailed savings proposals are still being developed through a three-year transformation programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has credible paths to close a gap of this size, whether it will require asset sales, further reserve draws, or government intervention.
findings.quote: our assessments of the budgetary impact of this uncertainty, within the latest review of our MTFP identifies a budget gap of £29.137m to 2030/31

findings.headline: Strategic pause on new reserve requests and review of existing commitments as a control measure
findings.detail: The council has introduced corporate spending controls in response to the Q1 deficit. It is freezing new reserve requests unless they are statutory, externally funded, or demonstrable invest-to-save schemes. The document states: "In response to the Quarter 1 forecast deficit, corporate controls have also been introduced, including a pause on new reserve requests and a review of existing commitments to protect the council's reserves position." This signals management recognition of financial stress.
findings.matters: A spending pause on non-essential commitments is a standard response to in-year deficit risk, but it is a sign of financial pressure and constrains the council's ability to invest in transformation or other priorities.
findings.figures: No specific figures, but £22.819m of earmarked reserves identified as available for budget resilience
findings.quote: In response to the Quarter 1 forecast deficit, corporate controls have also been introduced, including a pause on new reserve requests and a review of existing commitments to protect the council's reserves position.

findings.headline: Reserves fell by around 24% in 2024/25 and the council is now below peer resilience levels
findings.detail: Stockport's earmarked reserves dropped from £59.472m at March 2026 to £54.473m after the policy review and Q1 movements. The document cites CIPFA data: "Stockport held a reasonable level of reserves compared with other councils, but that these fell by around 24% during 2024/25." The comparison chart with other Greater Manchester councils shows Stockport at £59m against Rochdale (£152m), Bolton (£148m), and Tameside (£75m). The document acknowledges this means "the council's capacity to absorb further financial pressures" has been reduced.
findings.matters: Declining reserves in a council running deficits means less runway to weather further pressures. This directly affects borrowing capacity and credit risk.
findings.figures: Reserves fell 24% in 2024/25; Q1 2026/27 movement reduced reserves to £54.473m from £59.472m
findings.quote: Stockport held a reasonable level of reserves compared with other councils, but that these fell by around 24% during 2024/25. This reduction reflects the national decline in earmarked reserves and reinforces the need for the Reserves Policy to monitor both their adequacy and the rate at which they are used.

findings.headline: 2025/26 outturn was a deficit of £5.392m that required Budget Resilience Reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council could not balance its accounts in 2025/26 without drawing on reserves. This is not a one-off position: the Q1 forecast for 2026/27 shows a deficit of £8.334m, and the document explicitly states that "appropriate use of these reserves will be needed to support the balancing of the in-year deficit". The council is forecasting it will need to use reserves again to balance this year.
findings.matters: A council that cannot balance its budget without drawing reserves is burning financial resilience and has no buffer for unexpected pressures. Both lenders and the finance director need to know whether this is structural or temporary.
findings.figures: 2025/26 deficit £5.392m; Q1 2026/27 forecast deficit £8.334m
findings.quote: The council's 2025/26 outturn was a deficit of £5.392m prior to the use of Budget Resilience Reserves to balance the position at year end.

findings.paper_title: REPORT: Strategic Investment Assets: Scheme of Delegation
findings.headline: The Investment & Development Account relies on substantial annual reserve drawdowns to break even
findings.detail: The council's strategic investment property portfolio (Merseyway, Aurora, Cheadle Eco Park, Stockport Exchange) is not self-sustaining. The paper states that the I&D Account 'annually requires substantial support from the Council's reserves to ensure that it breaks even', indicating material structural weakness in investment property income relative to costs.
findings.matters: A council that cannot balance its investment property account without drawing reserves is consuming rather than building equity, signalling either failing asset performance or unsustainable cost structures that would concern any lender.
findings.figures: No specific annual drawdown amount stated; only that support is 'substantial' and 'annual'
findings.quote: The I&D Account annually requires substantial support from the Council's reserves to ensure that it breaks even.

findings.headline: Council operates within high-risk environment due to transformation programmes, ICT reliance, and emerging cyber/AI risks
findings.detail: The executive summary notes the council operates 'within a dynamic and evolving internal control environment, shaped by ongoing transformation programmes, delivery of the Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP), and increasing reliance on digital technologies. This has maintained a relatively high risk environment, particularly given organisational changes, evolving roles, and emerging risks such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.'
findings.matters: A high-risk control environment with ongoing transformation and heavy ICT reliance increases the risk of control failures, system outages, or cyber incidents that could disrupt services or expose data. Lenders assess operational resilience as part of credit quality.

findings.quote: The Council operates within a dynamic and evolving internal control environment, shaped by ongoing transformation programmes, delivery of the Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP), and increasing reliance on digital technologies. This has maintained a relatively high risk environment, particularly given organisational changes, evolving roles, and emerging risks such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence

findings.headline: Financial sustainability identified as one of four key ongoing governance challenges
findings.detail: The audit report identifies 'financial sustainability' as one of four broad areas requiring continued governance attention, alongside Transformation, Integrated Care, and Arm's Length Companies. This reflects sustained pressure on the council's finances.
findings.matters: Explicit identification of financial sustainability as an ongoing governance challenge indicates the council is operating under sustained financial pressure that requires continuous management focus and may limit service expansion or investment.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The review has identified and confirmed the following areas that will need to be addressed or continue to be addressed during 2025/26... Delivery of the Medium-Term Financial Plan

findings.headline: DOLS (Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards) audit found significant backlog with limited management information on case progress
findings.detail: The DOLS process audit received Limited Assurance, finding that despite good progress in system integration, 'a significant backlog remains, with limited management information on productivity, referrals, and case progress. This restricts effective resource planning and oversight.'
findings.matters: A DOLS backlog creates legal and safeguarding risk, and indicates either inadequate staffing or process efficiency issues requiring investment to resolve, which will have budget implications.
findings.figures: Significant backlog identified
findings.quote: A significant backlog remains, with limited management information on productivity, referrals, and case progress. This restricts effective resource planning and oversight

findings.headline: Ofsted downgrade of children's services from Good to Requires Improvement, citing demand and quality issues
findings.detail: In May 2025, Ofsted re-inspected children's services and downgraded from 'Good' (2022) to 'Requires Improvement', citing rising demand, deterioration in quality of social work practice, and delays in screening. The inspection rated overall effectiveness, leadership, child protection, and children in care as 'Requires Improvement'.
findings.matters: Ofsted downgrade signals deteriorating service quality and increased service demand that may drive unplanned budget pressures. Improvement plans will require investment; further deterioration could trigger regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: Downgraded from Good (2022) to Requires Improvement (May 2025)
findings.quote: Ofsted inspected Stockport Council's Children's Services, downgrading its overall effectiveness from 'Good' (2022) to 'Requires improvement'. Inspectors cited rising demand, a deterioration in the quality of social work practice, and delays in screening initial concerns

findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement remains in draft because 2025-26 Financial Accounts have not been formally signed off
findings.detail: The AGS is stated to remain 'in draft as the Council's 2025/26 Financial Accounts have not yet been formally signed off (as is the case with colleagues in Greater Manchester and wider)'. The report notes this is now July 2026.
findings.matters: Delayed financial accounts and unsigned AGS at this point in the financial year is unusual and indicates either restatements, audit adjustments, or significant issues requiring resolution before accounts can be certified.
findings.figures: July 2026 - accounts still not signed off
findings.quote: The current AGS remains in draft as the Council's 2025/26 Financial Accounts have not yet been formally signed off

findings.headline: Procurement partnership STAR failed to deliver agreed savings target of £1 million for 2024-25
findings.detail: Audit of STAR procurement service found that despite a stretch savings target of £1 million for all Greater Manchester partners, 'no financial savings were achieved for Stockport Council'. The audit gave Limited Assurance, citing operational oversight gaps and an expectations gap between the council and the shared service.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings from shared procurement affects the council's ability to meet MTFP targets and suggests procured services or savings initiatives may not be delivering expected financial benefits.
findings.figures: £1 million savings target for 2024-25, zero achieved
findings.quote: STAR faces a stretch savings target of £1 million for 2024–25 for all GM partner authorities, but no financial savings were achieved for Stockport Council

findings.headline: Homelessness services under severe financial pressure with rising costs dependent on government grant continuation
findings.detail: The audit of homelessness services received a Limited Assurance opinion, finding that rising demand and growing temporary accommodation costs place increasing pressure on the council's resources. The council remains 'heavily dependent on annual Central Government allocations to sustain delivery', meaning future funding uncertainty poses significant financial risk.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a demand-led service with escalating costs but limited control over demand. Dependency on central grants creates vulnerability if funding is reduced, potentially forcing unplanned service cuts or reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Rising demand, growing cost of temporary accommodation
findings.quote: The Council remains heavily dependent on annual Central Government allocations to sustain delivery. Recommendations to enhance tracking expenditure, reserves and developing a strategy to address future funding shortfalls, will reduce the Councils exposure to future financial risk, particularly if future grant levels are reduced or stagnate

findings.headline: Overall internal control environment rated as moderate assurance, indicating control weaknesses that put some objectives at risk
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's opinion provides moderate assurance, meaning the council has a 'generally sound system of internal control' but 'some weaknesses in the design and inconsistent application of controls put the achievement of particular objectives at risk'. This reflects a control environment that is functioning but with identified gaps.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance rather than substantial assurance indicates material control weaknesses exist that could affect the council's ability to deliver objectives and manage financial risk effectively.
findings.figures: Moderate assurance overall
findings.quote: some weaknesses in the design and inconsistent application of controls put the achievement of particular objectives at risk

findings.headline: Valuation of Manchester Airport Holdings Limited shareholding is based on management expert assumptions about financial performance and requires challenge
findings.detail: The council holds a shareholding in Manchester Airport Holdings Limited (MAHL) that is valued at fair value by a firm of financial experts. The valuation incorporates assumptions about financial performance, stability, and business projections. The audit team will engage internal property valuation experts to review the methodology and assumptions, but there is inherent uncertainty in the expert valuation.
findings.matters: A material misstatement in the MAHL valuation could affect asset values on the balance sheet. The valuation depends on airport financial recovery assumptions post-COVID, which carry significant uncertainty.
findings.figures: MAHL shareholding valued at fair value; valuation performed by BDO
findings.quote: The Council's shareholding in the Manchester Airport Holdings Limited (MAHL) has been valued by a firm of financial experts, engaged by management, based on assumptions about financial performance, stability, and key business projections. The figure disclosed in your accounts in relation to MAHL is at fair value.

findings.headline: Valuation of net defined benefit pension asset is complex, with pension asset ceiling calculation required under IAS19/IFRIC14
findings.detail: The council holds a net LGPS pension asset (as at 2024/25) and is required to calculate a pension asset ceiling under accounting standards IAS19 and IFRIC14. This is described as a complex calculation that caps the pension asset at a lower value. The valuation relies on actuarial assumptions including discount rate, inflation, and mortality rates. Greater Manchester Pension Fund's actuary provides the valuation, with triennial revaluation as at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: A material pension liability or unexpected ceiling adjustment could affect reserves and borrowing capacity. The complexity and materiality of the pension position make it a significant audit focus.
findings.figures: Pension asset (net) as at 31 March 2025; Greater Manchester Pension Fund triennial valuation dated 31 March 2025
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Council and its subsidiaries had a net LGPS Pension Asset and as a result the accounting framework required the actuary calculate a pension asset ceiling required under accounting standard IAS19 and IFRIC14. The pension asset ceiling is a complex calculation and caps the pension asset at a lower value.

findings.headline: Valuation of Land, Buildings and Dwellings requires full revaluation of council dwellings and new indexation methodology under revised CIPFA Code
findings.detail: 2025/26 is a full valuation year for all council dwellings. The CIPFA Code has been amended for 2025/26 to require land and buildings to be valued once every 5 years with annual indexation applied in intervening years. The council must apply judgement in selecting appropriate indices based on asset type, which introduces estimation uncertainty. The audit team will challenge the appropriateness of indices and test a sample of properties to confirm consistent allocation.
findings.matters: Property valuations directly affect the balance sheet position and could mask deterioration in the council's physical asset base. Index selection involves management judgement that could materially misstate asset values.
findings.figures: 2025/26 is full revaluation year for all council dwellings; rolling 5-year revaluation cycle with annual indexation
findings.quote: 2025/26 is a full valuation for all Council dwellings... The Code has been amended in 2025/26 and now requires land and buildings to be valued once every 5 years with annual indexation applied to assets during the four intervening years

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £64m, with statutory override expiring in March 2026
findings.detail: The DSG deficit was £43m at the end of 2024/25 and is forecast to grow to £64m by the end of 2025/26. A statutory override is currently in place to allow this deficit to be carried forward rather than funded from reserves, but it is due to expire in March 2026. The government has announced intentions to extend the override until 2028 while developing a sustainable solution, but this is not yet confirmed in law. If the override expires without extension, the council would be required to fund the deficit through reserves, which would significantly threaten financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A £64m reserve depletion would materially weaken the council's financial position and borrowing capacity, and represents genuine uncertainty about whether statutory obligations can be met without government intervention.
findings.figures: £43m deficit at end 2024/25; £64m forecast by end 2025/26; statutory override expires March 2026
findings.quote: The DSG deficit at the end of 2024/25 is £43m and is forecast to be £64m by the end of 2025/26. There is a statutory override in place which is due to expire in March 2026, although the government has announced its intentions to extend the override until 2028

findings.headline: Officers' conflicts of interest register incomplete due to competing resource demands
findings.detail: The council planned to complete a digital register of interests for officers serving on boards of wholly-owned companies (to manage conflicts of interest). This remains incomplete 'due to resource of the relevant colleagues being directed elsewhere', despite being flagged as important governance given risks of dual roles.
findings.matters: A council with multiple wholly-owned companies needs robust conflict-of-interest management. An incomplete register suggests governance processes are not fully implemented, particularly relevant given the identified risks of officers wearing multiple hats.
findings.figures: Digital register not finalised; resource redirected
findings.quote: The digital register of interests for officers has yet to be finalised due to resource of the relevant colleagues being directed elsewhere.

findings.headline: Emerging governance risk from AI decision-making without established oversight framework
findings.detail: The council identifies artificial intelligence as a new area of potential governance risk, noting concern about 'how its implementation may affect decision making'. An Ethics Board has been established with draft terms of reference, but has not yet met (first meeting scheduled for 2026/27).
findings.matters: Uncontrolled AI use in decision-making or financial analysis could create operational, reputational or compliance risks. For a lender, lack of governance over emerging technologies in financial or service decisions signals potential control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Ethics Board to hold first meeting in 2026/27
findings.quote: A new area of potential risk in relation to governance is emerging, as referred to above, in relation to AI and how its implementation may affect decision making.

findings.headline: Partner Integrated Care Board reported significant deficit with government-driven staffing cuts ahead
findings.detail: The Stockport Integrated Care Board, responsible for health and social care commissioning, reported a 'significant deficit' at year end. Government reforms are driving 'unavoidable cuts to staffing resources' during 2025-26, which the council flags as likely to impact 'quality of governance and decision making'.
findings.matters: A partner organization's deficit and staffing cuts can create unexpected demands on the council's finances and affect the quality of commissioned services. This introduces financial and operational risk to the council's position.
findings.figures: ICB reported 'significant deficit' at year end; two-phase voluntary redundancy programme ongoing
findings.quote: the ICB reported a significant deficit at year end

findings.headline: Significant savings requirement over next three years with funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council faces a requirement to find 'significant' savings over the next three years to maintain financial sustainability. This is framed alongside 'significant and urgent funding gaps which cannot be balanced' and increasing service demands for social care, homelessness, highways and other services.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to understand whether the council can deliver large savings while managing increased service demand. Unachieved savings targets would create further pressure on reserves and borrowing capacity.

findings.quote: the saving requirement the council needs to address in the next three years is significant

findings.paper_title: Stockport Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Final
findings.headline: Q1 2025-26 forecast shows £8.3m deficit with demand pressures expected to worsen during the year
findings.detail: The council's Q1 2025-26 forecast outturn is a £8.3m deficit. The auditor notes this is 'as the Council continued to deal with inflationary pressures and additional demand particularly for placements for looked after children'. Crucially, the council's own reporting made clear 'the adverse risk attached to its forecasts, and the likelihood of the deficit increasing as the year progresses due to the continued demand pressure and pricing'. This is an early warning that the 2025-26 budget (set to break even or use minimal reserves) is at material risk.
findings.matters: A £8.3m deficit forecast in Q1 signals the budget is already under pressure one quarter in, with demand trends expected to worsen. This suggests the full-year deficit will be significantly worse than budgeted unless major mitigations materialise.
findings.figures: Q1 2025-26 forecast deficit £8.3m, 2025-26 budget set with £0.4m minimal reserve use
findings.quote: The quarter one forecast outturn for 2025/26 was a deficit of £8.3m as the Council continued to deal with inflationary pressures and additional demand particularly for placements for looked after children.

findings.paper_title: Stockport Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Final
findings.headline: Net assets decreased £46m in a single year, driven by increased borrowings and property revaluations
findings.detail: The council's total net assets fell from £1,470m to £1,424m, a £46m year-on-year reduction. The auditor identifies this as driven by 'increases in borrowings, and decreases in the value of the Council's property, plant and equipment portfolio compared to the prior year'. The movements are described as 'in line with the Council's Treasury Management Strategy' and 'reflect the Council's capital programme', but a £46m swing in a single year signals significant capital activity and rising debt service costs.
findings.matters: Rising borrowings reduce financial flexibility and increase future revenue pressures from debt service. A £46m movement in net assets in one year indicates either aggressive capital spending or revaluation losses that should be monitored for trend.
findings.figures: Net assets decreased from £1,470m to £1,424m (£46m reduction), borrowings increased
findings.quote: The most significant changes in the balance sheet relate increases in borrowings, and decreases in the value of the Council's property, plant and equipment portfolio compared to the prior year.

findings.paper_title: Stockport Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Final
findings.headline: Reserves drawn down by £8m in 2024-25 with further projected drawdowns through MTFP period
findings.detail: Useable reserves fell from £144m to £136m during 2024-25, a net drawdown of £8m. The auditor's commentary notes multiple reserve uses including £2.9m from Income and Interest Rate Risk Mitigation, £1.5m from Revenue Contribution to Capital Outlay, and £0.9m each from Adults and Health/Social Care Integration. The council projects combined General Fund and earmarked reserves of £92m by end of 2025-26 — a further £44m reduction in two years. The MTFP runs to 2029-30, suggesting further pressure ahead.
findings.matters: Reserves are being used to balance budgets, not for genuinely one-off costs. If this trend continues through the MTFP, the council will face constraints on capacity to handle shocks and will have limited flexibility for borrowing or investment.
findings.figures: Reserves decreased £144m to £136m (2024-25), projected to be £92m (2025-26), multiple draws in year including £2.9m, £1.5m, £0.9m from individual reserves

findings.headline: Children's services overspend of £8.78m in 2024-25 with demand pressures forecast to continue into 2025-26
findings.detail: Children's services delivered an overspend of £8.78m in 2024-25 as part of a total service budget deficit of £10.55m. The auditor notes 'ongoing demand pressures in children's services' and the Q1 2025-26 forecast shows a £8.3m council-wide deficit driven by 'additional demand particularly for placements for looked after children'. This is a structural issue, not a one-year variance. Ofsted inspected children's services in May 2025 and rated them as 'requires improvement', with the council approving £1.2m of reserves to fund an improvement plan.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in this service area have persisted year-on-year and are forecast to continue. The Ofsted rating adds regulatory pressure and reputational risk. The council is now drawing reserves to fund improvement, indicating staffing or service redesign costs ahead.
findings.figures: Children's services overspend £8.78m (2024-25), total service deficit £10.55m, Q1 2025-26 forecast deficit £8.3m, £1.2m reserves approved for improvement plan

findings.paper_title: Stockport Council - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Final
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £64m by March 2026 with statutory protection due to expire
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew to £43m by end of 2024-25 and is forecast to rise to £64m by end of 2025-26. This is driven by uncontrollable demand pressures, particularly in SEND and high-needs placements where council costs exceed the ring-fenced government grant. A statutory override currently shields this from the council's general reserves, but that protection expires in March 2026. While government has indicated intentions to extend the override to 2028, if it does not, the council will be forced to absorb the deficit through its useable reserves.
findings.matters: This is an existential financial sustainability risk. If the override ends and is not renewed, the council faces forced drawdowns of £64m+ from reserves that currently total £136m. This would severely constrain financial flexibility and capacity to borrow or invest.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £43m (2024-25), forecast £64m (2025-26), statutory override expires March 2026, council useable reserves £136m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The position is unsustainable and without significant additional external funding support, improved prevention and changes to delivery models are needed.

findings.headline: Capital programme is 68% spent by Q3, accelerating cash depletion and financing needs
findings.detail: Capital expenditure reached £111.730m by 31 December, representing 68% of the annual budget of £163.300m. This rapid pace of capital deployment is the primary driver of investment balance depletion and the need for external borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement stands at £934.803m.
findings.matters: Fast capital delivery may signal strong regeneration momentum, but it also creates persistent financing needs. Combined with minimal liquidity by year-end, any acceleration in planned spending or cost overruns could force the council to borrow on unfavourable terms.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure: £111.730m (68% of £163.300m budget) to 31 December 2025. CFR: £934.803m.
findings.quote: As of 31 December 2025, capital expenditure reached £111.730m, representing approximately 68% of the annual budget

findings.headline: Investment income underperforming budget by 20 basis points (£64k shortfall projected)
findings.detail: The council budgeted for investment returns of 4.10% but now projects 3.90%, representing a 20 basis point negative variance. This translates to a projected income shortfall of approximately £64k (£1.248m actual vs £1.312m budgeted). The shortfall is driven by Bank Rate cuts that arrived one quarter earlier than the original February 2025 forecast.
findings.matters: Even modest revenue shortfalls compound in a tight fiscal environment. The variance also indicates the council's budget assumptions were overly optimistic about interest rates, raising questions about forecasting reliability for other assumptions.

findings.quote: the projected annual return of 3.90% represents a 20-basis-point negative variance against the original budget of 4.10%

findings.headline: Net debt increased by £16.7m to £784.095m, with borrowing costs rising
findings.detail: Net debt rose from £767.417m at mid-year to £784.095m by Q3, an increase of £16.7m. The consolidated cost of borrowing increased from 3.80% to 3.82%. This rising net debt reflects the combination of temporary borrowing increases and accelerated capital programme spending.
findings.matters: Rising net debt, even if within prudential limits, indicates increasing leverage. A lender must track whether the upward trend continues and whether the capital programme remains manageable within the council's debt capacity and affordability ratios.
findings.figures: Net debt: £767.417m (mid-year) to £784.095m (Q3). Borrowing cost: 3.80% to 3.82%.
findings.quote: Net debt rose between the mid-year point of 2025/26 and the conclusion of quarter 3, increasing from £767.417m to £784.095m. The consolidated cost of borrowing across the General Fund and the Housing Revenue Account stands at 3.82%, a marginal increase from the 3.80% reported on 30 September 2025

findings.headline: Temporary borrowing surged £28m in one quarter at rising rates (4.09% to 4.18%)
findings.detail: Temporary borrowing increased from £112.500m to £140.500m between mid-year and Q3, a £28m jump in three months. The borrowing rate also rose from 4.09% to 4.18%. This sharp increase in expensive short-term debt reflects seasonal year-end liquidity pressures in the inter-authority market, but it signals rising short-term financing costs.
findings.matters: Temporary borrowing at 4.18% is far more expensive than the 1-3 year PWLB rates the council targets (4.27%-4.52%). High temporary borrowing suggests liquidity stress and wastes treasury resources on costly short-term funding.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing: £112.500m (mid-year) to £140.500m (Q3). Rate: 4.09% to 4.18%.
findings.quote: This movement is attributed to an uptick in temporary borrowing, rising from £112.500m to £140.500m, and a concurrent increase in investments from £36.575m to £47.505m. The temporary borrowing rate shifted from 4.09% at the end of September to 4.18% by 31 December 2025

findings.headline: Investment balances depleting to minimal levels by year-end, forcing shift from internal borrowing toward external financing

This requires accessing PWLB or other external markets for quarter 4 borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council retains adequate liquidity and borrowing capacity. Minimal cash buffers reduce financial flexibility and signal the council will need sustained external access to capital markets to fund its capital programme.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £47.505m (Q3), forecast £14.750m average (Q4), then minimal by 31 March 2026. Capital expenditure £111.730m through Q3.
