findings.detail: The council explicitly states it faces 'a recent increase in demand for the use and maintenance of historic buildings within the borough' and that 'current costs exceed the available budgets.' The council is now exploring grant funding and repurposing opportunities to address the gap.
findings.matters: Council-owned historic assets (including listed properties and civic buildings) show unfunded maintenance pressure; signals either deferred maintenance or need for major capital injection.
findings.figures: Costs exceed available budgets (specific variance not quantified)
findings.quote: There has been a recent increase in demand for the use and maintenance of historic buildings within the borough. In response, we are actively exploring maintenance programs and refurbishment opportunities to repurpose and revitalise these buildings, as current costs exceed the available budgets.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Capital Strategy and Capital Programme - Appendix One
findings.headline: School estate condition backlog of £121m to £240m against annual investment of only £6.2m
findings.detail: The council identifies a rolling programme of condition surveys showing approximately £121m of condition capital need (potentially £240m if estate is to meet modern building regulations and environmental standards). Investment in condition for 2026/27 is planned at £6.2m. This represents a structural gap between identified need and annual investment rate.
findings.matters: Unmet school maintenance needs pose operational risk and eventual large capital requirement; significantly underfunded backlog suggests deferred problems that lenders should understand.
findings.figures: £121m identified backlog (potentially £240m), £6.2m annual investment in 2026/27, approximately £65m of backlog relates to roofing, mechanical and electrical schemes
findings.quote: The School Estate has a backlog of around £121m condition capital need identified from the rolling programme of condition surveys. This could be as high as £240m if the replacement or repaired estate is to provide a modern learning environment and meet new building regulations and rising building indices since the assessments were made.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection deficit of £0.969m driven by 10% surge in mental impairment exemptions linked to ageing population
findings.detail: The Collection Fund shows Council Tax deficit of £0.969m at Q2+. A 10% increase in exemptions for individuals with severe mental impairment (SMI) is a primary driver. The council notes 'Given Stockport's relatively older population, the borough may be disproportionately affected by this exemption which could further contribute to the Council Tax deficit.' Additionally, second homes dropped 21% since introduction of premium, reducing income.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a core, relatively stable funding source. A trend toward rising exemptions driven by demographic change (ageing population) suggests structural income pressure likely to persist. This is not a temporary variance but a reflection of the resident demographic the council serves.
findings.figures: £0.969m Council Tax deficit, 10% increase in SMI exemptions, 21% decrease in second homes income
findings.quote: Recent data shows a 10% increase in dwellings occupied by individuals who are eligible for severe mental impairment (SMI) exemption. Given Stockport's relatively older population, the borough may be disproportionately affected by this exemption which could further contribute to the Council Tax deficit.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £66m by March 2026, costing £2.3m/year in borrowing costs, with no sustainable solution after statutory override ends 2027/28
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) high needs block shows Q2+ forecast deficit of £22.845m, part of cumulative £66m deficit by 31 March 2026. This costs the council £2.3m/year in borrowing costs (£5m cumulatively since 2019/20) to cash flow the shortfall. The statutory override allowing councils to hold DSG deficits outside the General Fund extends to end of 2027/28, after which DSG must be funded from General Fund. Government support post-override is 'conditional and not open-ended.'
findings.matters: The £66m DSG deficit represents 63% of total reserves (£95m). When the statutory override ends in 2027/28, the council must eliminate this or incorporate it into General Fund budgets, likely requiring substantial additional borrowing or further reserve depletion. This is a material long-term financial risk dependent on government reforms that may not materialise.
findings.figures: £22.845m Q2+ deficit, £66m cumulative by March 2026, £2.3m annual borrowing cost, £5m cumulative since 2019/20
findings.quote: The Quarter 2+ forecast outturn position is a deficit of £22.845m... Holding this deficit on the balance sheet is costing the council's General Fund around £2.3m in-year (around £5m cumulatively since 2019/20) in borrowing costs to cash flow the underfunded position on the DSG high needs block.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £4.526m persists and worsened Q2 to Q2+, with cost reductions plateauing
findings.detail: Adult Social Care forecasts £4.526m deficit (3.3% of budget), up £0.155m from Q2. The £1.974m overspend from 2024/25 has carried into 2025/26. Although bed-based care numbers reduced versus 2024/25, 'the reduction has now plateaued rather than continuing a downward trend, as initially anticipated.' Demand for homecare and complexity of clients in Supported Accommodation continues increasing.
findings.matters: This is a recurrent overspend in a demand-led service, now in its second year. The plateau in reductions means cost-control strategies are not delivering expected benefits, suggesting the budget pressure is structural rather than cyclical and will likely recur in 2026/27.
findings.figures: £4.526m deficit, £1.974m carryover from prior-year overspend, £0.155m deterioration Q2→Q2+
findings.quote: The Quarter 2+ forecast outturn position for the Health, Wellbeing and Adult Social Care portfolio is a deficit of £4.526m which represents 3.3% of the portfolio cash limit budget of £138.549m. This is an increased overspend of £0.155m on the Quarter 2 forecast... the reduction has now plateaued rather than continuing a downward trend, as initially anticipated.

findings.headline: SEN transport demand up 22.6% in 18 months with costs rising 28% (from £7.076m to £9.073m), a statutory obligation the council cannot avoid
findings.detail: Special Education Needs transport shows sharp demand growth: 985 pupils in April 2024 rising to 1,209 by September 2025, with Full Year Cost growing from £7.076m to £9.073m. The council cites 'growth/demand in the system, new/replacement contracts at higher price points, loss of charity non-profit organisations offering services and the complexity of arranging bespoke pupil packages' as drivers. This is a statutory requirement; councils cannot refuse to provide SEN transport.
findings.matters: This is a demand shock in a non-discretionary budget. The council cannot control numbers or easily reduce unit costs. The 28% increase in cost over 18 months suggests the trend will continue, making this a material medium-term budget pressure independent of local management.
findings.figures: 985 pupils April 2024 → 1,209 September 2025; £7.076m FYC → £9.073m FYC
findings.quote: April 2024: 985 pupils / 342 routes – Full Year Cost (FYC) at £7.076m... September 2025: 1,209 pupils and FYC at £9.073m.

findings.headline: Revenue deficit of £7.653m requires drawing on reserves to balance, with Council explicitly stating this is not sustainable
findings.detail: The council forecasts a revenue deficit of £7.653m at Q2+, comprising £11.490m deficit in cash limit portfolios partially offset by £3.217m surplus in non-cash budgets. Balancing the position will require use of one-off resources and reserves. The report states explicitly that 'the continued reliance on reserves and one-off resources is not sustainable and presents an opportunity cost, potentially impacting other council priorities and ambitions.'
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial resilience would be concerned that the council operates deficits requiring reserve drawdown rather than within means. Total reserves fell from £102.293m to £95.051m in Q2+ alone (£7.2m reduction), suggesting reserves could be exhausted in 2-3 years if structural deficits persist.
findings.figures: £7.653m revenue deficit, £11.490m cash limit deficit, reserves fell £7.2m in Q2+ alone
findings.quote: The Quarter 2+ forecast outturn position for the council's revenue budget is a deficit of £7.653m... balancing the in-year position at year end will require the use of available one-off resources and reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The Capital Financing Requirement (the accounting measure of the council's underlying debt need) is projected to reach £959.834m by end of 2026/27, constrained by a fixed 50-year MRP repayment schedule.
findings.detail: The council's total CFR is growing from £937.652m (current estimate) to £959.834m in 2026/27 and trending downward to £938.862m by 2028/29 (assuming MRP repayments outpace new borrowing). Of this, £137.988m is historic debt being repaid over 50 years (ending March 2065) under the old RSG-supported regime. MRP charges are £33.268m annually.
findings.matters: A CFR of nearly £1bn shows the scale of the council's indebtedness. The 50-year repayment schedule commits the council to £3.538m annual MRP payments until 2065, constraining budget flexibility for decades.
findings.figures: Total CFR £959.834m (2026/27); Non-HRA CFR £796.075m; HRA CFR £163.759m; annual MRP charge £33.268m (2026/27); historic debt £137.988m repaid over 50 years to March 2065
findings.quote: General Fund borrowing that historically received central government support via the Revenue Support Grant (RSG) system will be provided for using equal annual instalments over a standard 50-year period, commencing on 1 April 2015. As at the effective date of 1 April 2026, the outstanding value of this borrowing stands at £137.988m, equating to an equal annual minimum revenue provision of £3.538m; the final instalment for which is scheduled to be provided no later than 31 March 2065.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The council's core operating cost from capital investment (Council Tax impact) is £34.34 per Band D property in 2026/27, which is material and front-loaded.
findings.detail: The 'incremental impact of capital investment decisions' on Council Tax Band D is £34.34 in 2026/27, dropping to £2.78 in 2027/28 and £4.77 in 2028/29. This front-loading reflects the borrowing costs hitting the revenue budget immediately as capital projects commence, while the benefits (if any) accrue gradually.
findings.matters: A material, front-loaded Council Tax increase signals to residents and the market that the council's capital ambitions carry real revenue consequences. This can constrain future budget headroom if the capital investments do not generate offsetting income or savings.
findings.quote: Incremental impact of capital investment decisions on the Band D council tax: 2026/27 £34.34

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The council is foregoing long-term fixed-rate borrowing to wait for lower rates, betting that interest rates will fall materially by late 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council's borrowing strategy is one of 'prudent delay,' deliberately avoiding locking in long-term PWLB debt now (rates 4.6%-5.8% for 5-25 years) in anticipation that rates will be 'more favourable' by late 2026. The council is prioritising short-term borrowing (under 5 years, where rates are lower) and targeting 2027 for long-term fixed-rate borrowing. This depends on the interest rate forecast being correct.
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as forecast (due to persistent wage growth, geopolitical shocks, or fiscal pressures), the council will have delayed borrowing at more affordable rates and may face higher costs later. The strategy also increases exposure to refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Current 5-year PWLB rate 4.60%, 10-year 5.20%, 25-year 5.80%; forecast to fall to 5-year 4.10%, 10-year 4.70%, 25-year 5.30% by end Q4 2027
findings.quote: Consequently, our strategy is one of prudent delay. We are avoiding locking into expensive, long-term debt now in anticipation of a more favourable long-term interest rate environment in the future. However, we remain vigilant: global bond markets continue to experience volatility as investor confidence fluctuates between 'safe-haven' government bonds and riskier assets.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The council has committed £100m as an equity and loan facility for town centre regeneration (MDC strategy) as part of capital spending.
findings.detail: Within the £152.732m capital expenditure, the council has approved 'a recyclable equity and loan facility of £100m to support the MDC delivery strategy' for town centre development. Equity investments carry greater risk than loans because they rank behind debt in repayment hierarchy. The document notes this will have 'a subsequent impact on the council's prudential indicators, in particular the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR).'
findings.matters: Equity investments in commercial property/regeneration schemes are riskier than traditional council borrowing for infrastructure or housing. Property values and development returns can be volatile, and losses would hit the council's balance sheet directly.
findings.figures: £100m equity and loan facility for MDC; total capital expenditure including this £152.732m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The council has approved significant prudential borrowing to support this capital investment which includes a recyclable equity and loan facility of £100m to support the MDC delivery strategy.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The council has £100m of PWLB borrowing maturing in 2026 that must be refinanced at current elevated rates.
findings.detail: In early 2025, Stockport borrowed £187m from PWLB in two tranches. The first tranche of £100m matures between June and November 2026 at an average rate of 4.73%. Refinancing this requires either securing new borrowing at potentially different rates or using available cash. The council identifies this as its 'immediate focus for 2026.'
findings.matters: A £100m refinancing in a volatile interest rate environment is a material near-term risk. If rates rise sharply or market conditions deteriorate, refinancing costs could spike significantly.
findings.figures: £100m maturing June-November 2026 at average rate 4.73%; second tranche £87m in 2027/28 at average rate 4.87%
findings.quote: Members will recall in early 2025, the council successfully secured £187m from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) during a period of short-term market illiquidity. To mitigate 'refinancing risk' (the danger of having to renew large amounts of debt all at once during a spike in interest rates), the council split this borrowing into two manageable tranches: £100m maturing between June and November 2026 (avg. rate 4.73%).

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Strategy and Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
findings.headline: The council is moving from under-borrowing to external financing for the first time in years as capital plans exceed internal reserves.
findings.detail: The council has used internal cash reserves to fund capital projects while remaining 'under-borrowed' (underborrowed by £80.152m as at 31 March 2026). With £152.732m capital expenditure planned for 2026/27, internal resources no longer suffice. The document states this will 'mark a strategic shift' requiring the council to 'externalise a portion of our internal debt, transitioning from using our own cash to taking on new external loans.'
findings.matters: The shift to sustained external borrowing will increase interest costs for the council's revenue budget and raises questions about whether these capital investments are truly affordable over time.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing £80.152m (31.03.26); capital expenditure £152.732m in 2026/27; total CFR £959.834m by end of 2026/27
findings.quote: 2026/27 will mark a strategic shift. We expect to 'externalise' a portion of our internal debt, transitioning from using our own cash to taking on new external loans (both short and long-term) to ensure our investment projects are fully funded and delivered.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation cost pressures growing: £1.923m recurrent investment added to budget for Place directorate.
findings.detail: The MTFP records £1.923m of additional recurrent budget pressure in the Place directorate, with 'main cost increases in Homelessness, Temporary Accommodation and Parking.' These are noted as ongoing in-year pressures requiring permanent budget uplift. The council is not presenting this as a temporary spike but as persistent demand.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs are notoriously difficult to control and are growing nationally. Permanent budget additions suggest the council sees this as structural demand, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £1.923m recurrent impact on Place budgets
findings.quote: The MTFP update includes £1.923m increase in the service budgets in recognition of the recurrent impact of the budgetary pressures being realised in-year. The main cost increases in Place are in Homelessness, Temporary Accommodation and Parking.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Projected reliance on Council Tax increases: government assumes 4.99% annual CT rises; by 2028/29, 66% of council's Core Spending Power will come from Council Tax, not government grant.
findings.detail: The provisional settlement assumes councils will increase Council Tax by the maximum allowable 4.99% each year (3% general + 2% ASC precept). By 2028/29, the council's projected resources show 66% of CSP will be funded by Council Tax rather than government grant. The S151 officer recommends assuming 4.99% annual increases in the MTFP planning assumption, but the cumulative effect is that around £13m of the Council Tax increase will be offsetting the reduction in government grant funding rather than funding new services.
findings.matters: Shifting the funding burden to residents is politically difficult and has limits (band limits, referendum requirements). For a council in a challenging deprivation profile, a 4.99% annual CT rise compounds residents' cost-of-living pressures. Failure to deliver these rises would deepen the saving requirement.
findings.figures: 66% of 2028/29 CSP projected from Council Tax by 2028/29; £39m additional CT income assumed by 2028/29; £13m of CT increase offsetting grant reduction rather than funding services
findings.quote: The council's increase assumes it will raise additional Council Tax income of around £39m by 2028/29, meaning 66% of the council's CSP by 2028/29 will be funded by Council Tax rather than government grant funding. This also means around £13m of the assumed Council Tax income increase is offsetting the reduction in government grant funding over the settlement rather than being directed to fund local services.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk acknowledged as growing: S151 officer says it is 'unlikely in the short term' but 'does not understate the significant and critical financial challenge'; LGA warns more councils may need Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: The council's S151 officer states: 'the likelihood of having to issue a Section 114 notice in the short-term period remains unlikely but does not understate the significant and critical financial challenge facing the council.' However, the document repeatedly emphasises the council is 'pushing closer to needing to ask for exceptional financial support from government' and notes that 'the adverse impact of the settlement is pushing the council closer to having to ask government for this.' The LGA is warning that more councils may need emergency bailouts, and the language in this report positions Stockport as at risk.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals financial distress and inability to set a balanced budget. The fact that this risk is now explicitly mentioned—even if 'unlikely'—indicates the council has crossed a threshold where insolvency is a named possibility rather than theoretical.
findings.figures: S151 officer statement that S114 remains 'unlikely in the short term'; council acknowledged as 'pushing closer' to needing EFS
findings.quote: The council's Section 151 Officer believes the likelihood of having to issue a Section 114 notice in the short-term period remains unlikely but does not understate the significant and critical financial challenge facing the council.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: 2025/26 in-year forecast outturn deficit of £7.653m (3.95% service budget overspend); mitigated only by drawing on reserves and one-off resources.
findings.detail: The current financial year (2025/26) is forecast to end with a deficit of £7.653m. This comprises a £11.490m deficit on service cash limit budgets, partially offset by corporate budget surpluses. The 3.95% overspend on service budgets at the start of the year indicates structural overspend, not temporary pressure. The council is managing this through 'One Council One Budget' recovery work and spend control, but 'balancing the in-year position at year end will require the use of available one-off resources and reserves.'
findings.matters: A £7.6m deficit in the current year shows the council is already unable to live within its budget. The need to raid reserves to balance a single year's accounts, while planning for £14.8m savings next year, is not sustainable.
findings.figures: £7.653m deficit forecast 2025/26; £11.490m service budget deficit; 3.95% overspend on service budgets
findings.quote: As reported in the 2025/26 Quarter 2+ Budget Monitoring Update presented elsewhere on this agenda, the forecast outturn position for the council's revenue budget is a deficit of £7.653m. The deficit is made up of a projected £11.490m deficit on service cash limit budgets, offset by a projected £3.217m surplus on non-cash corporate budgets and a £0.620m surplus on general financing.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Adult social care demand pressures worsening: Stockport is oldest locality in Greater Manchester with 85+ population projected to rise 36% over next 10 years.
findings.detail: Stockport has 20.1% of population aged 65+ (compared to 15.7% across GM). The 85+ population has grown 20% in the last decade and is projected to grow 36% over the next 10 years. The council is budgeting £2.050m additional recurrent investment in 2026/27 for Adult Social Care and expects further pressures from complex younger adults transitioning from children's services. The MTFP assumes a 'left shift' approach will produce savings by 2027/28-2028/29, but no savings are yet achieved.
findings.matters: An ageing population creates structural, growing demand for social care. Unlike demand that might reduce, this demographic trend is irreversible over the medium term. Service demand will grow faster than the council's funding.
findings.figures: 20.1% of Stockport population aged 65+; 2.9% aged 85+; 85+ population projected to rise 36% over next 10 years to 12,000; £2.050m additional recurrent budget 2026/27
findings.quote: Stockport is the 'oldest' locality in Greater Manchester, and along with much of the country, Stockport's population continues to age. The population aged 85+ has grown by 20% in the last 10 years (up by 1,500 people) and is projected to rise by 36% over the next 10 (reaching 12,000).

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Children's Services Ofsted rating downgraded from 'good' in May 2025; looked-after children numbers up 13% in three years; external placements rising in cost.
findings.detail: In May 2025, Ofsted downgraded the council's Children's Services from the previous 'good' rating. The number of looked-after children has grown to 508 in June 2025, a 13% increase since June 2022. More significantly, external placements (highest-cost option) have risen from 26% of CIC service costs in June 2022 to 29% in June 2025. The council is budgeting £7.856m additional recurrent investment in this service in 2026/27 and targeting a reduction of placement numbers by 100 by 2028/29 as an MTFP assumption—acknowledged as 'a challenging target given the ever-increasing need for support and complexity of that need'.
findings.matters: Downgraded Ofsted ratings typically lead to increased costs as councils recruit to address improvement plans. Rising looked-after children numbers and increasing cost per placement suggest demand is outpacing mitigation. The council's own forecast reductions by 2028/29 are ambitious targets, not achieved reductions.
findings.figures: 508 looked-after children (June 2025); 13% increase since June 2022; external placements 26% of costs (June 2022) rising to 29% (June 2025); £7.856m additional recurrent budget 2026/27; target reduction of 100 placements by 2028/29
findings.quote: In May, the council's Children's Services were inspected by Ofsted resulting in a downgrading of the previously received rating of 'good'. The number of CIC in June 2025 was 508, a 13% increase since June 2022. External placements (EP) (placements run by external providers both in Stockport and in other areas) which are the highest cost, have risen as a percentage of overall CIC service costs. In June 2022 EPs were 26% of the CIC service costs. In June 2025 EPs were 29% of the CIC service costs.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: High-needs DSG deficit forecast at £66m by end of 2025/26; statutory override ends March 2028 with write-off details still unconfirmed.
findings.detail: The council's cumulative DSG deficit is forecast to reach around £66m by end of financial year. While a statutory override allows councils to hold historic deficits unrealised on the balance sheet, the council still bears the cash flow borrowing costs to fund the unfunded education spend—£2.3m in 2025/26 alone. Government has promised support via write-off when the override ends in March 2028, but 'detail of what this support will be are yet to be released.' This creates uncertainty about a £66m liability.
findings.matters: This represents a £66m hidden liability. When the override expires, the council may face demands to resolve the deficit or face continued annual borrowing costs. The absence of confirmed government support makes this a contingent liability with unknown resolution.
findings.figures: £66m cumulative DSG deficit; £2.3m borrowing costs in 2025/26; override ends March 2028
findings.quote: The council's cumulative deficit is forecast to be around £66m by the end of the financial year. While councils await a permanent solution to the historic underfunding of this important education spend, a government directed statutory override is in place. This allows councils to hold their historic deficits on their balance sheet unrealised. This does however have a significant impact on councils' general fund budget because of the cash flow borrowing costs to fund the unfunded education spend.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Cumulative savings requirement reaches £68.6m by 2029/30, starting from £14.8m in 2026/27; change proposals identify only £8m of savings.
findings.detail: The MTFP shows annual saving requirements growing from £14.8m in 2026/27 to reach cumulative £68.6m by 2029/30. The council has only identified £8.037m of change proposals to contribute to this, of which £6.537m relies on unspecified 'productivity and efficiency' savings. The document explicitly acknowledges risk: 'There is always a risk that the change proposals identified following further work are no longer robust, achievable, or accepted by the council.'
findings.matters: A savings requirement of this scale, growing year-on-year with limited identified solutions, signals a council in structural deficit. Only 8% of the 2026/27 gap is covered by named proposals; the remainder depends on either unachieved efficiencies or one-off resources.
findings.figures: £14.812m saving requirement 2026/27; £33.446m 2027/28; £53.673m 2028/29; £68.610m 2029/30; £8.037m change proposals identified
findings.quote: Following the MTFP Update adjusting the underpinning forecasts and assumptions set out in this report, the council has a £14.812m saving requirement in 2026/27 rising to £68.610m in 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Part B - Medium Term Financial Plan Landscape and Forecast 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Fairer Funding Review produces significantly worse settlement than expected: core spending power rises only 7.49% to 2028/29 against England average of 15.1%.
findings.detail: The 'fairer funding' outcome has created a £22.5m reduction in Settlement Funding Assessment over the three-year settlement period. The council will receive a total adverse impact of £12.5m by 2028/29 from changes to the formula. Funding per resident by 2028/29 will be £1,229 compared to England average of £1,440. The council has been excluded from recovery grant funding that other similar councils receive, losing £7.8m in redistributed funding and missing out on £10m in funding increase protection guarantees.
findings.matters: A council's baseline funding is the foundation of financial sustainability. This settlement makes Stockport progressively less well-funded relative to peers facing identical service demands, forcing either tax rises or service cuts.
findings.figures: 7.49% CSP increase by 2028/29; England average 15.1%; £22.5m SFA reduction; £12.5m adverse MTFP impact by 2028/29; £7.8m lost from recovery grant exclusion; £10m lost from funding increase protection guarantee
findings.quote: The council's core spending power will increase by 7.49% (a £26m increase) by 2028/29 compared to an England average increase of 15.1%. Funding per resident by 2028/29 is £1,229 compared to the England average of £1,440.

findings.headline: Council's increasing commercial activity through subsidiary companies adds financial complexity and governance risk
findings.detail: The council notes that increased powers around commercialism have led to it becoming 'increasingly complex, including the creation of subsidiary companies.' Directly funded borrowing is being used for commercial ventures like Totally Local Company (£1.396m fleet vehicle loan facility) and Adswood Depot redevelopment serving as TLC's operational base. The capital strategy explicitly flags this as requiring full understanding of 'residual risks and liabilities' to which the council is subject.
findings.matters: Subsidiary company structures and commercial investments create contingent liabilities and governance complexity that lenders need to understand. If commercial ventures underperform, the council may be required to support them from revenue, impacting debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £1.396m loans to Totally Local Company for fleet vehicles; £2.784m Adswood Depot redevelopment; total commercial element not quantified
findings.quote: Increased powers around commercialism have led to the council becoming increasingly complex, including the creation of subsidiary companies. It is vital that those tasked with governance fully understand the financial risks that the council is exposed to, including the residual risks and liabilities that it is subject to.

findings.headline: HRA new housing development adding £57m capital investment pending Cabinet approval
findings.detail: Four new HRA housing schemes (London Road Extra Care, Romiley Liberal Club, Sunfield, Andrew Street phase 2) will deliver 202 new homes and add approximately £57m to the capital programme over three years. This includes £24m of Homes England and Brownfield grant funding. The schemes have been added to the 2026/27 programme pending formal approval, indicating significant committed investment contingent on that approval.
findings.matters: A substantial new capital commitment contingent on approval represents execution risk if approval is delayed or withdrawn. The scale (£57m) is material to the council's total capital programme and debt position.
findings.figures: £57m total scheme cost over three years; £24m Homes England and Brownfield grant funding; 202 new homes across four sites; £13.949m added to 2026/27 programme pending approval
findings.quote: This scheme will deliver 202 new homes in four new housing developments, London Road Extra Care, Romiley Liberal Club, Sunfield and Andrew Street phase 2. The scheme will add circa £57m to the capital programme over the next three years, which includes £24m of Homes England and Brownfield grant funding, and the schemes have been added to the 2026/27 capital programme to ensure that this substantial scheme is reflected pending approval.

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing finances 36% of the three-year capital programme, a substantial debt-funded capital investment approach
findings.detail: Of the £225.844m total three-year capital programme, £55.45m is funded by prudential borrowing (£50.778m directly funded borrowing and £4.672m unsupported borrowing). This means the council is borrowing heavily to fund capital investment across regeneration, housing, schools and service infrastructure.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on prudential borrowing to fund capital expenditure tests the council's ability to service debt from revenue. Lenders need to understand whether the capital investments generate sufficient returns or savings to service the borrowing costs within existing revenue budgets.
findings.figures: £50.778m directly funded borrowing (2026/27); £4.672m unsupported borrowing (2026/27); 36% of three-year programme total
findings.quote: Prudential borrowing (directly funded and corporate unsupported borrowing) makes up 36% of the resources funding the three-year capital programme.

findings.headline: Stockport Crematorium requires capital investment to address building and equipment condition issues
findings.detail: The capital programme allocates £4.344m in directly funded borrowing for the crematorium to address condition issues with its buildings and equipment. This indicates an asset in poor condition requiring substantial remediation.
findings.matters: An operational asset in poor condition requiring substantial capital injection signals potential maintenance backlogs elsewhere in the estate. This is relevant to the council's asset management strategy and long-term capital requirements.
findings.figures: £4.344m directly funded borrowing in 2026/27; additional £2.5m in 2027/28 and £1.745m in 2028/29 allocated
findings.quote: £4.344m in directly funded borrowing for Stockport Crematorium, which is a large scale scheme to address the condition issues with the buildings and equipment.

findings.headline: Weir Mill regeneration project has structural damage and requires additional borrowing beyond original facility
findings.detail: Weir Mill, a £69.652m total regeneration scheme in the Town Centre West area, has suffered structural issues that delayed completion. The council now needs to increase the debt finance facility funding the scheme to complete it, with practical completion rescheduled for 31 March 2026. This is a material scope change requiring new approval.
findings.matters: A major regeneration project encountering structural problems and cost overruns signals delivery risk. The need for additional borrowing mid-project and schedule delay are material concerns for lenders evaluating the council's capital delivery capacity.
findings.figures: £69.652m total scheme cost; £10.833m directly funded borrowing in 2026/27 capital programme
findings.quote: Weir Mill is a large ongoing regeneration development with a total scheme cost of £69.652m. Structural issues within the mill buildings have delayed the scheme, with practical completion now scheduled for 31 March 2026. As a result, it is necessary to increase the current debt finance facility funding the scheme, which is presented for approval elsewhere on this agenda.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns council is being pushed toward requesting exceptional financial support from government
findings.detail: The Director of Finance states: 'While we wish to avoid having to ask government for exceptional financial support, the proposed funding in the provisional settlement is pushing us closer to this.' This is a formal alert that the council is approaching a tipping point where it may need government bailout or special status assistance to remain solvent.
findings.matters: A lender must regard councils requesting or receiving exceptional support as materially higher credit risk. This statement is a yellow flag that the council's own finance leader sees the current trajectory as unsustainable without intervention.
findings.figures: No specific figures; this is a forward-looking assessment.
findings.quote: While we wish to avoid having to ask government for exceptional financial support, the proposed funding in the provisional settlement is pushing us closer to this.

findings.headline: Use of one-off reserves (£4.485m in 2026/27) to balance budget signals deferred problems and eroding financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council drew £4.485m from earmarked budget resilience reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget. It adds back only £0.710m to the workforce investment reserve (funded from pension contribution savings). The budget narrative explicitly cautions that over-reliance on reserves 'simply pushes budget pressures and saving requirements to later years' and notes that reserves should not be used to avoid difficult decisions. The minimum recommended general fund balance (£15.183m) is being held at current levels but is not growing.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover recurrent spending gaps is unsustainable and signals eroding financial resilience. A lender needs to track whether reserves are being depleted, and whether the council will have capacity to absorb an unexpected shock (inflation spike, care demand surge, capital project overrun) without service disruption or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Reserves drawn 2026/27: £4.485m. General Fund Balance held at minimum: £15.183m (no growth forecast). Corporate contingency budget released: £11.436m.
findings.quote: We note and agree with the Section 151 Officer's caution about the risk an over reliance on the use of reserves to support the budget presents to longer term financial robustness and resilience. This simply pushes budget pressures and saving requirements to later years.

findings.headline: Structural social care pressures with £8.3m additional funding for adult social care and £3.2m for children's services in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council allocated £8.257m contingency to Adult Social Care and £3.179m to Children, Families and Education in 2026/27 to fund inflationary costs, demographics, and demand increases. The budget narrative identifies specific pressures: children in care placements rising, complexity of needs driving up external placement costs, adults social care demand from younger adults with mental health and learning disability needs, and homelessness rising with shortage of affordable housing. These are recurrent pressures, not one-time.
findings.matters: Social care is a large proportion of Stockport's spend (74.1% of all service spend supports vulnerable residents). Demographic and need-driven pressures are structural and growing, not cyclical. A lender needs confidence these can be managed within available resources or whether they will become chronic overspends that force reserves to be drawn or services to be rationed.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care contingency 2026/27: £8.257m; Children, Families & Education contingency: £3.179m. Social care and public health represent 74.1% of all service spend.
findings.quote: Ever-increasing need for support, complexity of that support and inflationary costs continue to put significant financial pressure on the delivery of local services, particularly those services supporting our most vulnerable residents.

findings.headline: Council Tax dependency unsustainably high: by 2028/29, 66% of core spending power will be from local taxpayers, not government
findings.detail: Stockport has implemented a 4.99% Council Tax increase (2.99% general + 2% ASC precept) to fund 2026/27, and the MTFP assumes continued 4.99% increases through 2028/29. By 2028/29, £13m of the assumed Council Tax increase is merely offsetting government funding cuts. The council's own commentary describes this as 'unsustainable' and a 'regressive form of taxation' that masks government failure to fund services adequately.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance of revenue stability. High reliance on Council Tax increases is regressive and politically difficult to sustain. High deprivation areas (Stockport has four wards in the 1% most deprived nationally) may face collection risks if residents cannot afford 5% annual increases. Resistance to future rises could force service cuts or debt.
findings.figures: 4.99% Council Tax increase 2026/27; 66% of CSP from Council Tax by 2028/29 (vs government-funded services); £13m of assumed Council Tax increase by 2028/29 offsetting grant reductions
findings.quote: By 2028/29, 66% of our CSP is from Council Tax paid by Stockport taxpayers rather than government funding. We are extremely disappointed by government's continuation to place burden on local taxpayers to fund local services.

findings.headline: Large medium-term savings requirements (£12m–£23m annually from 2027/28) signal major service reductions ahead and growing budget stress
findings.detail: The council faces cumulative savings requirements of £12.2m in 2027/28, £20.8m in 2028/29, and £23.5m in 2029/30. The 2026/27 budget is only balanced through £4.485m of one-off reserve drawdown and £8.037m of savings proposals (parking, SEN transport, corporate restructuring). The narrative acknowledges that achieving these savings will require redesigning service operating models and potentially stopping some services entirely.
findings.matters: These figures reveal a council in structural deficit that cannot be closed through efficiency alone. A lender needs to know whether the council will have appetite or political capacity to cut statutory services (social care, children's) to meet these targets, or whether it will exhaust reserves and become dependent on government support or debt.
findings.figures: Savings requirement 2027/28: £12.172m; 2028/29: £20.799m; 2029/30: £23.452m. One-off reserves used 2026/27: £4.485m. Total change proposals 2026/27: £8.037m.
findings.quote: The saving requirement in 2027/28 onwards is significant. While we are confident about the robustness of our proposed balanced budget in 2026/27, the saving requirement in 2027/28 onwards is significant.

findings.headline: Stockport uniquely excluded from Recovery Grant Guarantee, losing £10m of funding protection that other metropolitan councils receive
findings.detail: Only three metropolitan borough councils outside London lack the Recovery Grant Guarantee. This costs Stockport approximately £10m in funding protection over the settlement period, plus £7.8m in needs-assessed funding that would have been distributed if the £600m Recovery Grant had been incorporated into the settlement. The council explicitly states this is impossible to reconcile with fairness.
findings.matters: This is an unexplained anomaly that signals higher fiscal risk. If Stockport's exclusion is a policy error, a reversal could improve finances; if intentional, it represents entrenched disadvantage. Either way, a lender needs confidence in the council's advocacy and the government's stability of funding policy.
findings.figures: £10m funding protection lost; £7.8m needs-assessed funding not received
findings.quote: More critically we are one of only three metropolitan borough councils outside London not to receive the associated Recovery Grant Guarantee. This means Stockport also loses out on around £10m of funding increase protection over the settlement.

findings.headline: Government fairer funding settlement worsened the MTFP by £12.5m and left Stockport £254 per head below comparable councils
findings.detail: Stockport's core spending power increases only 7.49% by 2028/29, against an England average of 15.1%. The fairer funding review redistributed money away from Stockport: CSP per head of £1,229.24 vs £1,483.59 for average metropolitans, and £1,435.44 for Reading (similar IMD score). The council claims it would receive £76.9m more if it had received the metropolitan average settlement.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council's financial position is sustainable; this settlement signals structural underfunding relative to comparable councils with similar deprivation and service demands, raising questions about whether the council can service debt.
findings.figures: £22.5m total loss of government grant; £12.5m worsening of MTFP by 2028/29; CSP increase 7.49% vs 15.1% England average; £254.35 per head shortfall vs metropolitans
findings.quote: For Stockport the outcome is worrying, a total loss of government grant through the settlement funding assessment based on the updated assessment of need of £22.5m over the settlement, and a £12.5m worsening of the MTFP forecasts by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Temporary borrowing from other councils has risen sharply (£57.5m increase) due to PWLB maturing debt and cash flow strain, making the council dependent on a market known to be tightening.
findings.detail: Total debt rose from £792.044m to £803.992m, driven by 'a significant increase in temporary borrowing of £57.5m largely due to PWLB borrowing maturing loans repaid in Quarter 1 of £45m'. The council has not undertaken any long-term borrowing in 2025/26 so far. This reliance on temporary/rolling short-term debt exposes the council to refinancing risk as the local-to-local market is acknowledged to be in shortage.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing can be rolled or replaced only if counterparties are willing to lend. The report flags this may not be possible during 'liquidity shortages' and warns the council may struggle to 'secure financing for critical projects'. A rollover crisis would force emergency PWLB borrowing at inopportune rates.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing increased £57.5m; PWLB maturing debt repaid £45m in Q1; no long-term borrowing undertaken in first half 2025/26
findings.quote: a significant increase in temporary borrowing of £57.5m largely due to PWLB borrowing maturing loans repaid in Quarter 1 of £45m

findings.headline: Government debt issuance is forecast to quadruple (£180bn), a 'flood' likely to keep long-term gilt yields and PWLB rates elevated despite Bank Rate cuts.
findings.detail: The report cites MUFG commentary that 'a flood of government debt issuance (circa £180bn which is a four-fold increase) could lead investors to demand higher interest rates.' Despite forecasts for Bank Rate to fall to 3.25% by end of 2026, gilt yields (and thus PWLB rates) may remain elevated due to structural supply pressure from government borrowing. The 50-year gilt yield reached 5.98% at 30 September 2025, highest since 1998.
findings.matters: This decouples PWLB rates from Bank Rate cuts—a local authority borrowing at a 25-year maturity in 2026 may face rates higher than today even if Bank Rate is cut to 3.25%. The council cannot simply wait for Bank Rate to fall and expect cheaper long-term borrowing.
findings.figures: Government debt issuance forecast at £180bn (four-fold increase); 30-year gilt yield reached 5.7% (highest since 1998); 50-year PWLB at 5.98%
findings.quote: MUFG commentary noted that a flood of government debt issuance (circa £180bn which is a four-fold increase) could lead investors to demand higher interest rates

findings.headline: Investment income is expected to fall materially as interest rates decline, adding pressure to the revenue budget at a time the council is trying to close a £19m+ deficit.
findings.detail: The council achieved 4.28% return on investments in the first half of 2025/26 but acknowledges 'The current return of 4.28% at the mid-year point will reduce as we progress through the second half of the financial year, as investment rates are now lower than the start of the financial year.' The report explicitly warns 'Lower investment income from falling interest rates could negatively impact the revenue budget' and that this must be accounted for when 'forecasting the MTFP and closing the budget gap.'
findings.matters: As Bank Rate falls from 4% toward 3.25%, money market funds (the council's primary vehicle) will yield progressively less. This removes an offset to rising treasury costs at precisely the moment the council is trying to save £19m in 2026/27.
findings.figures: Current investment return 4.28%; budgeted return 4.10%; forecast Bank Rate 3.25% by end of 2026; average investment duration 3.66 days
findings.quote: Lower investment income from falling interest rates could negatively impact the revenue budget. The strategy must account for this reduction in income when forecasting the MTFP and closing the budget gap.

findings.headline: The council has a £19.162m savings requirement for 2026/27, part of a larger £63m budget gap projected by 2029/30.
findings.detail: As of September 2025, the council has identified specific savings required for the next financial year, with a growing deficit trajectory. The report notes 'increasing demand for services, particularly in adult and children's social care and homelessness, coupled with inflationary pressures' as key drivers. A Council Tax increase of 4.99% was already taken in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A cumulative £63m budget gap over four years (2026/27–2029/30) signals structural fiscal stress. Growing demand pressures and limited tax flexibility indicate the council may struggle to meet obligations without further service cuts or extraordinary measures.
findings.figures: £19.162m savings requirement for 2026/27; £63m total budget gap by 2029/30; 4.99% Council Tax increase in 2025/26
findings.quote: the council has identified a £19.162m savings requirement for 2026/27, which is part of a larger £63m budget gap projected by 2029/30

findings.headline: The council faces tightening access to short-term borrowing and is increasingly reliant on PWLB as the local authority lending market contracts.
findings.detail: The report states 'A shortage of available funds in the local-to-local market means that securing a loan may be more challenging and more expensive' and that 'A combination of factors is driving shortages and elevated rates in the short-term local authority (LA) lending market'. The council may now need to 'explore longer-term borrowing options from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB)' and acknowledges 'recent financial difficulties and Section 114 notices at other authorities' are affecting market sentiment.
findings.matters: Constrainment in local-to-local lending forces councils to borrow at higher PWLB rates or defer projects. The reference to Section 114 notices suggests reputational contagion from other councils' financial distress is pricing the council out of cheaper alternatives.
findings.figures: PWLB 5-year rates averaged 4.82%; 25-year rates averaged 6.11%; 50-year rates averaged 5.83%
findings.quote: A combination of factors is driving shortages and elevated rates in the short-term local authority (LA) lending market in the 2025/26 financial year. For the council as a borrower, this means facing higher costs and increased difficulty securing financing for critical projects during this period.

findings.headline: The council is re-phasing capital schemes and delaying borrowing to manage exposure to elevated interest rates.
findings.detail: A total of £59.418m of capital schemes have been moved to later years from 2025/26, including £12.476m for Cheadle Eco Business Park, £8.594m for SEMMMS Relief Road, and £6.661m for Weir Mill. This re-phasing is explicitly stated to 'reduce the cost of borrowing impacted by the current high interest rates'. The original borrowing requirement of £72.097m has been cut to £45.046m.
findings.matters: Capital deferrals signal the council is prioritising near-term borrowing cost avoidance over delivery timetables, suggesting it is materially cost-constrained. This affects both its ability to execute planned investment and its medium-term financial plans.
findings.figures: £59.418m re-phased; borrowing requirement reduced from £72.097m to £45.046m; 30-year PWLB rates reached 6.23% at 3 September 2025
findings.quote: officers are reviewing the Capital Programme to identify capital scheme spending profiles which can be rephased to later years to reduce the cost of borrowing impacted by the current high interest rates

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset from April 2026 will increase retained business rates funding requirement but quantum of impact remains uncertain
findings.detail: Government will reset councils' Business Rates Baselines from April 2026, increasing the proportion of business rates each council must retain to fund its assessed funding need. The council will have to cover any shortfall in business rates collection above the Government's safety net threshold. The council is holding a Business Rates Reset reserve to mitigate this risk, but notes it will 'continue to be monitored at each annual review as Government provide further clarity' on the actual impact.
findings.matters: A material change to the funding model in 2026/27 creates income risk if business rates collection underperforms; the council currently has limited visibility on the true scale of exposure.
findings.figures: Business Rates Reset reserve held (specific amount not disclosed in this paper); 2025/26 expected retention benefit from GM Trailblazer Deal is £6.370m
findings.quote: Government will reset councils' Business Rates Baselines from April 2026. This presents a financial risk to the council as a greater proportion of Business Rates collected from businesses will be expected to be retained to fund its assessed funding need... For this reason, a Business Rates Reset reserve continues to be held to mitigate this risk and smooth any financial impact. This will continue to be monitored at each annual review as Government provide further clarity on their intentions.

findings.headline: Council warns that drawing reserves to cover deficits will cripple investment capacity and render capital schemes unaffordable
findings.detail: The council explicitly cautions that 'sustained and significant short-term use of earmarked reserves to support the council's financial robustness and resilience will have a severe impact'. Growth and reform projects are 'underpinned by the resources held in earmarked reserves'; drawing these significantly will force reliance on borrowing, potentially rendering 'projects and investments no longer financially viable to proceed due to the borrowing costs and resulting financial risk'. Reserves are essential to 'the affordability of capital schemes' where borrowing is needed.
findings.matters: The council is warning that using reserves to patch deficits will eliminate its ability to invest and transform, creating a potential spiral of declining resilience and rendering its growth strategy unachievable.
findings.figures: £25.718m total reserves currently supporting investment plans; no quantum disclosed for capital scheme viability threshold
findings.quote: The council's planned projects and investments supporting its growth and reform ambitions for the borough are underpinned by the resources held in earmarked reserves. Having to significantly use these resources will require alternative sources of funding to be identified (i.e. borrowing) to support these plans. In some cases, it will render the projects and investments no longer financially viable to proceed due to the borrowing costs and resulting financial risk.

findings.headline: Council explicitly planning to draw up to £25m from earmarked reserves to cover budget deficits whilst seeking permanent solutions
findings.detail: The council has realigned £25.718m of reserves to support financial resilience, comprising £16.517m earmarked specifically 'to mitigate financial risk over the medium term'. The policy explicitly contemplates that 'if needed resources held in earmarked reserves can be uncommitted to meet funding gaps over the medium-term period'. The council recommends a limit of £25m on reserve draws for financial resilience before requiring further approval, pending identification of 'permanent funding options'.
findings.matters: Planned reserve depletion signals the council does not expect to balance budgets through operational measures alone and is relying on one-time reserve draws, which reduces future financial flexibility and indicates unresolved structural budget deficits.
findings.figures: £25.718m reserves available for financial resilience; £16.517m specifically earmarked to mitigate financial risk; recommended limit on reserve draws: £25m before requiring further Cabinet approval
findings.quote: Following the annual review, realignment of resources held has provided a total of £25.718m of reserves to support the council's financial resilience and robustness... it is recognised that if needed resources held in earmarked reserves can be uncommitted to meet funding gaps over the medium-term period... It is recommended that the use of earmarked reserves to support the council's financial resilience over the medium term is limited to £25m (as set out above) before requiring further approval.

findings.headline: Structural demand-led and inflationary pressures creating volatile, sustained budget stress in children's and adults services
findings.detail: The council identifies 'increasing need for support and inflationary costs' as continuing to place 'significant pressure' on essential services, particularly 'demand-led services supporting our most vulnerable residents'. The Reserves Policy allocates £18.656m to mitigate these pressures, with the explicit rationale that these services face 'highly volatile cash limit budgets due to demand and inflationary pressures' and there is 'a risk that the Service Areas experiencing these budget pressure have a structural budget deficit position going forward'.
findings.matters: Structural demand-led deficits in children's and adults services cannot be solved by one-time measures and indicate long-term funding challenges that the council is unable to resolve through its own efficiency savings.
findings.figures: £18.656m held in reserves specifically to mitigate demand-led budget volatility (£15m as risk-related commitments, £2.139m approved commitments)
findings.quote: Despite the council's strong financial management, increasing need for support and inflationary costs continue to put significant pressure on the delivery of essential services to residents and businesses. This is particularly evident for those demand-led services supporting our most vulnerable residents... Without these reserves being available there is a risk that the Service Areas experiencing these budget pressure have a structural budget deficit position going forward and impact on the council's ability to set a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Council ending 2024/25 with a small deficit, now holding General Fund Balance £0.060m below the Section 151 Officer's assessed risk minimum
findings.detail: The council's 2024/25 outturn was a deficit of £0.060m, funded by using the General Fund Balance. This leaves the General Fund Balance at £15.123m. However, the Section 151 Officer's annual risk assessment has determined that the minimum prudent level should be £15.183m. The council is therefore starting 2025/26 with a General Fund Balance that is £0.060m below its own risk-assessed minimum.
findings.matters: A General Fund Balance below the Section 151 Officer's assessed minimum reduces the council's buffer to absorb unexpected costs or revenue volatility, especially material given the Q1 deficit forecast.
findings.figures: 2024/25 outturn deficit: £0.060m; General Fund Balance held: £15.123m; assessed minimum required: £15.183m
findings.quote: The council's 2024/25 outturn position was a deficit of £0.060m. This was funded by a corresponding use of the General Fund Balance at year end as required by legislation for Local Government accounting. As a result, the council has a General Fund Balance of £15.123m as at 31 March 2025. The Section 151 Officer's risk assessment for 2025/26 identified a required General Fund Balance of £15.183m.

findings.headline: Significant in-year budget deficit forecast for Q1 2025/26 requiring emergency corporate intervention
findings.detail: The council's Q1 2025/26 budget monitoring (reported separately) shows a significant in-year forecast deficit. The council has mobilised its Corporate Leadership Team to ensure heightened corporate oversight, with the Reserves Policy flexibility expected to be critical to managing this whilst permanent solutions are developed. The paper explicitly states this is a material near-term challenge requiring active management.
findings.matters: A significant in-year deficit requiring emergency corporate response indicates the baseline budget is not sustainable and that planned savings or efficiency measures have not closed the identified gap.
findings.figures: Significant in-year forecast deficit (quantum referenced in separate Q1 budget monitoring report, not disclosed here)
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Quarter 1 budget monitoring, presented elsewhere on this agenda, presents a significant in-year forecast deficit. An immediate response to the forecast has been put in place led by the Corporate Leadership Team to ensure even greater corporate oversight to recover and mitigate costs.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: Investment portfolio compressed to 11.68 days average duration, down from 37.49 days; Q4 averaged just 1.09 days
findings.detail: The council's average investment duration collapsed from 37.49 days in 2023/24 to 11.68 days in 2024/25, with Q3 and Q4 averaging only 1.56 and 1.09 days respectively. The council explicitly states it could not use diversified "laddered investments" due to liquidity constraints. Average investment balances also fell from £46.7m to £36.4m, signalling reduced cash reserves available for investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess the council's liquidity and cash reserves. The collapse to near-overnight holdings suggests the council is operating with tight cash management and limited financial buffer, indicating vulnerability to unexpected cash demands.
findings.figures: Average duration: 37.49 days (2023/24) to 11.68 days (2024/25); Q3: 1.56 days, Q4: 1.09 days; average balance £46.671m to £36.422m
findings.quote: As liquidity requirements were a drain on day-to-day investment choices, extending duration through the use of 'laddered investments' (investments placed in tranches of varying amounts and varying maturity dates aimed at extending the duration and return of portfolio) was not possible.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: Mandatory IFRS16 leases accounting added £13.7m to council's Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: First-time adoption of IFRS16 Leases standard in 2024/25 increased the CFR by £13.690m, capitalising lease assets that were previously expensed. This is a one-time impact but permanently increases the council's stated debt burden, as the leases will be amortised over their asset life.
findings.matters: A lender must account for this increase when assessing the council's debt levels and borrowing capacity. While not new borrowing, it increases the stated CFR against which debt limits are measured.
findings.figures: £13.690m increase to CFR
findings.quote: The impact of this is an increase in the capital financing requirement of £13.690m, and this will be written down over the lifetime of the asset.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: General Fund capital programme underspent by £21.3m (19% below budget); major Weir Mill scheme rephased by £19.6m
findings.detail: The council budgeted £115.1m for General Fund capital expenditure but spent only £93.9m; HRA similarly underspent (£40.1m budget vs £23.9m actual). The primary driver was rephasing of schemes to later years, with the Weir Mill Development alone accounting for £19.6m of the shortfall. This suggests either execution risk or a slowdown in investment plans.
findings.matters: A lender assesses the council's capital programme delivery capability. Large rephasing (particularly of major economic development schemes like Weir Mill) suggests project risk or changes in investment priorities. The pattern also delayed the borrowing requirement, which then had to be compressed into Q4.
findings.figures: GF budget £115.147m, actual £93.870m (£21.3m underspend); HRA budget £40.108m, actual £23.875m; Weir Mill rephased £19.632m
findings.quote: The decrease in General Fund prudential borrowing from £53.424m in the budget capital programme for 2024/25 to £31.657m at outturn is largely due to a number of re-phased schemes to later years; most notably £19.632m for Weir Mill Development.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: Council has no access to alternative long-term funding sources; entirely dependent on PWLB
findings.detail: The report states that alternative borrowing sources simply do not exist for the council in current market conditions. The only option outside PWLB is bond issuance, which the council has not undertaken. This leaves the council with no flexibility if PWLB rates become prohibitively expensive or if PWLB access is curtailed.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council's funding options under stress. Total dependence on a single source (PWLB) is a structural vulnerability.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Opportunities to take long term loans from alternative market participants were absent during 2024/25, unless the council had considered bond issuance.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: Short-term lending market collapsed; rates spiked to over 6% by February 2025, forcing council away from temporary borrowing strategy
findings.detail: From Quarter 3 2024/25 onwards, liquidity shortages in local authority short-term lending markets caused rates to escalate dramatically. By February 2025, short-term rates were "far in excess of 6%" while Bank Rate stood at 4.5%. This eliminated the council's preferred strategy of temporary borrowing and forced the switch to longer-dated PWLB debt. The council explicitly noted it was "aware of its reliance on internal cash reserves and the availability of short-term loans from other councils."
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can continue to refinance if short-term markets remain dysfunctional. The council's treasury strategy has depended on temporary borrowing availability; loss of that access exposes it to forced long-term borrowing at disadvantageous rates.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 4.5%; short-term local-to-local rates "far in excess of 6%" by February 2025
findings.quote: Short-term local to local rates continued to rise and were considerably more elevated than Bank rate. By February 2025 levels were far in excess of 6% and were expected to continue to rise to the end of March.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2024/25 Main Report
findings.headline: Council took £187m PWLB borrowing in February–March 2025 at 4.80% average rate to address market liquidity crisis
findings.detail: The council borrowed £187m in twelve tranches during the final quarter of 2024/25, split to mature £100m in 2026/27 at 4.73% average and £87m in 2027/28 at 4.87% average. This was a direct response to short-term lending markets becoming inaccessible at normal rates. The council had anticipated needing to refinance maturing loans and fund capital programmes but was forced by market conditions to lock in longer-dated debt at elevated cost.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's access to capital markets and whether it faces refinancing risk. This borrowing decision was driven by market stress rather than planned capital investment, and locks in above-historical borrowing costs for years.
findings.figures: £187m total; £100m maturing 2026/27 at 4.73%; £87m maturing 2027/28 at 4.87%; overall average 4.80%
findings.quote: A total amount of £187m was borrowed from the PWLB in twelve tranches during February and March 2025 and split between financial years to mature £100m in 2026/27 (average rate 4.73%) and £87m in 2027/28 (average rate 4.87%).

news_drafts.headline: The council is using one-off resources to balance each year, with a 2025/26 outturn deficit of £7.839m and a 2026/27 Q1 forecast deficit of £8.489m
news_drafts.lead: The use of reserves to balance budgets signals the underlying position is not sustainable. If one-off resources are being used year-on-year, reserves are a stopgap, not a strategic buffer. The council's minimum reserve level means there is little headroom…

news_drafts.headline: Core Spending Power increases by only 7.53% over the settlement period, compared with 15.52% nationally and 19.7% for comparable metropolitan boroughs, a structural funding gap
news_drafts.lead: This is a funding gap that local efficiency cannot close. The council cannot grow its way out of this — it is a structural allocation decision. The gap persists across the medium term and means the council is permanently worse funded than peers.

news_drafts.headline: SEND transport demand increased 58% in four years (1,243 pupils at June 2026 vs ~786 in June 2022), with limited tools to arrest growth
news_drafts.lead: SEND transport is a General Fund pressure driven by identification of need and is not easily reducible. The council's mitigations (travel training, shared routes) are marginal. The 58% growth in four years shows acceleration.
